title: Impact of Dosage Modifications on Efficacy: Insights from Select Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitors Approved for Treatment of Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer with EGFR Mutations.
authors: Carrasquilla SD, Bi Y, Gu W et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Dosage modifications, including dose interruptions and reductions, are commonly implemented to manage adverse reactions observed with oncology drugs. However, their impact on efficacy is not well understood. Here, we explored the impact of dosage modifications on progression free survival (PFS) and overall survival (OS) for four US FDA-approved tyrosine kinase inhibitors for the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) mutations.
METHODS: We collected patient-level data from clinical trials supporting the original FDA approvals of afatinib, dacomitinib, mobocertinib, and osimertinib. We identified the daily dose received (DDR; a measure of the dosage received by a patient each day), dose interruptions and reductions over the treatment period. In this exploratory analysis, we used a time-dependent Cox proportional hazards model to assess the impact of DDR on PFS and landmark time-fixed Cox models at 30, 60, and 90 days from treatment initiation to assess the impact of early dose interruptions and reductions on PFS and OS.
RESULTS: While the impact of dose interruptions and reductions on the risk of death varied among the studied drugs, dose interruptions, such as interruptions for four or more consecutive days, were more often associated with a higher risk of progression or death than dose reductions.
CONCLUSION: For the evaluated drugs as monotherapy in NSCLC with EGFR mutations, our analysis suggests that dose reductions might have a lower impact on efficacy than missing or interrupting treatment. Further studies are needed to evaluate other EGFR treatments, drug classes, and cancer types.

title: TAVO412, an Anti-EGFR, cMET and VEGF Trispecific Antibody: Initial Results from a Phase I Dose Escalation Study in Patients with Advanced Solid Tumors.
authors: Han C, Xie H, Yu Y et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: We report the results of a Phase 1 study of TAVO412, an anti-EGFR, cMET, and VEGF-A multi-specific antibody.
PATIENTS AND METHODS: Patients of age ≥18 years with advanced solid tumors refractory to standard therapies were enrolled (TAVO412-CN001, NCT06761651). The study used a standard 3 + 3 design for dose-escalation from 150 to 1500 mg every two weeks in a 28-day cycle. Patients were backfilled for further assessment of safety and preliminary anti-tumor activities.
RESULTS: The study included 67 patients, with 6 tumor types. Serum drug exposures increased with the dose. TAVO412 had low immunogenicity (5.9%). No DLTs were reported and the MTD was not reached up to 1500 mg. The most common treatment-related (TR) AEs (≥30%) across all doses were rash, hypoalbuminemia, stomatitis, infusion related reaction, increased ALT, and hypokalemia. Preliminary anti-tumor activities were observed in NSCLC patients (n = 27) with 5 PRs (3 of 9 EGFR Exon20ins and 2 of 12 Exon21 L858R) and 13 SDs, in ESCC (n = 11) with 1 PR and 8 SDs, and in CRC (n = 15) with 4 PRs and 7 SDs, in the dose range from 750 to 1500 mg. All PRs were confirmed except 1. The longest treatment duration was approximately 39 weeks. Baseline soluble VEGF-A levels correlated with treatment responses.
CONCLUSIONS: TAVO412 was tolerated up to 1500 mg, with mostly target-related AEs. Preliminary activities of TAVO412 were observed in CRC, ESCC, and NSCLC patients who had been heavily treated. Further evaluation of TAVO412 in patients with these tumor types is warranted.

title: RNA-Adjusted TUFM Protein State Captures Mitochondrial Proteome Organization in Lung Adenocarcinoma.
authors: Weng X, Tang Y, Li Q et al.
abstract: Matched transcriptome-proteome measurements can reveal protein-state information not represented by RNA abundance. We integrated four lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) proteogenomic cohorts, two longitudinal osimertinib transcriptomic systems, and DepMap CRISPR screens to test whether the TUFM protein captures coordinated mitochondrial proteome organization beyond TUFM RNA. In discovery LUAD, the RNA-adjusted TUFM protein state (TUFM_PT) added substantial explanatory information beyond its transcript for mitochondrial-translation and oxidative-phosphorylation (OXPHOS) protein programs. Across three independent cohorts (n = 292), TUFM_PT replicated with pooled Spearman rho values of 0.564 and 0.620 for mitochondrial translation and OXPHOS, respectively, and ranked 40th and 23rd among 5,242 externally benchmarked RNA-adjusted protein states. Associations persisted after copy-number, clinical, tumor-purity, and background-proteome adjustment. Highest-ranked human TUFM_PT proteomic partners were enriched in an independent CRISPR codependency network, including after the exclusion of prespecified mitochondrial genes, demonstrating cross-modal convergence at the network tail. Longitudinal osimertinib data provided complementary temporal context: early drug tolerance suppressed mitochondrial translation and OXPHOS transcripts, followed by later recovery without universal TUFM mRNA recovery. Together, these findings identify TUFM_PT as a reproducible, network-embedded proteomic readout of mitochondrial organization beyond TUFM RNA, while the longitudinal transcriptomes define the treatment-stage context rather than treatment-linked TUFM protein dynamics.

title: High Neuronal PAS Domain Protein 2 Expression Associated with Poor Prognosis, Tumor Immune Infiltration, and Adenosine Pathway Markers in Lung Cancer.
authors: Dai J, Reyimu A, Song X et al.
abstract: This study aims to explore the clinical significance of neuronal PAS domain protein 2 (NPAS2) in lung cancer, its relationship with the tumor immune microenvironment, and its potential upstream non-coding RNA (ncRNA) regulatory network. By analyzing transcriptomic data and clinical information from the Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) database, prognostic genes were identified, and NPAS2 expression was analyzed in lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma to determine its associations with patient survival and immune cell infiltration. Immunohistochemical analysis was also performed to compare NPAS2 expression between lung cancer tissues and adjacent non-tumor tissues. NPAS2 expression was elevated in tumor tissues, with higher expression associated with reduced overall survival. This association remained significant in multivariate Cox regression analysis (hazard ratio (HR) = 1.11687, P = 0.0252). In the analyzed dataset, a diagnostic model incorporating NPAS2, epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), marker of proliferation Ki-67 (MKI67), and tumor protein p63 (TP63) yielded an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.987. Immune infiltration analysis revealed that in lung adenocarcinoma and lung squamous cell carcinoma, NPAS2 expression was positively correlated with CD4⁺ T cell and neutrophil infiltration, as well as with the expression of the immune checkpoint molecule sialic acid-binding immunoglobulin-like lectin 15 (SIGLEC15). Additionally, NPAS2 expression was positively correlated with the adenosine pathway markers CD39 and CD73. Bioinformatics analysis further identified a potential regulatory axis of NORAD/AC087477.2-hsa-miR-106a-5p/hsa-miR-17-5p-NPAS2. These results suggest that NPAS2 may be a candidate biomarker for lung cancer diagnosis and prognosis assessment and may be associated with tumor immune cell infiltration and adenosine-related immune regulatory processes. However, further functional experiments and clinical validation are needed to clarify its potential molecular mechanism and clinical application value.

title: Expert Consensus Recommendations on NSCLC Management: Evidence-Based Strategies for Early Resectable and Locally Advanced Disease from Asia.
authors: Soo RA, Sachithanandan A, Higgins KA et al.
abstract: Lung cancer remains the most common malignancy in Asia and is characterised by a substantial proportion of cases occurring in never-smokers, a feature that distinguishes the region from many Western populations. Only 20-25% of patients with newly diagnosed non‑small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) present with resectable disease. As precision oncology expands into earlier stages, understanding how global standards can be adapted to Asian healthcare systems is increasingly important. This expert consensus report summarises evidence-informed opinions and voting outcomes from 13 lung cancer specialists across 11 countries to identify regional priorities, practical implementation needs, and management strategies for early and locally advanced NSCLC. Experts supported annual low‑dose CT (LDCT) screening for high‑risk individuals, with adaptation of criteria to better capture Asia's substantial burden of never‑smokers and individuals with strong family history. Early diagnostic pathways emphasised rapid tissue acquisition and timely biomarker testing specifically EGFR, ALK, and PD‑L1 at initial diagnosis for both resectable and unresectable disease. Across resectable stage II-III disease, evidence from multiple Phase III trials consistently demonstrates that integrating immunotherapy with neoadjuvant or perioperative chemotherapy improves pathological response and event‑free survival, while maintaining surgical feasibility. Differences between regimens relate largely to timing, agent selection, and biomarker effects, and practical adoption in Asia varies according to diagnostic capacity and local resource availability. For unresectable stage III NSCLC, concurrent chemoradiotherapy followed by consolidation durvalumab remains standard, while recent data from the LAURA trial support consolidation osimertinib after CRT for EGFR-mutated disease, with a marked progression-free survival benefit (HR 0.16). Shared regional gaps include limited screening uptake, variable reimbursement for molecular testing and targeted therapies, and uneven access to multidisciplinary care. Collectively, the available evidence suggests that earlier biomarker testing, structured nodule management pathways, and broader access to perioperative and consolidation therapies can meaningfully improve outcomes in Asian populations. Strengthening MDT integration and harmonising diagnostic and therapeutic workflows across settings remain essential next steps.

title: SUMOylation counteracts ubiquitination to stabilize ANKRD1 and promote osimertinib resistance in lung adenocarcinoma.
authors: Fan B, Lei Q, Wang H et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Acquired resistance to osimertinib remains a major challenge in the treatment of EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD), yet the contribution of stress-responsive protein homeostasis to resistance remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to investigate the role and regulatory mechanisms of ankyrin repeat domain 1 (ANKRD1) in acquired osimertinib resistance.
METHODS: Public transcriptomic datasets and machine learning-based feature selection were integrated with osimertinib-resistant LUAD cell models, paired clinical specimens, RNA sequencing, biochemical and molecular assays, functional rescue experiments, and in vivo tumor models to investigate the role of ANKRD1 and its upstream and downstream regulatory mechanisms in osimertinib resistance.
RESULTS: ANKRD1 was upregulated in osimertinib-resistant LUAD models and promoted tumor cell survival under therapeutic pressure. Mechanistically, zinc finger protein 593 (ZNF593) interacted with ANKRD1 and facilitated its SUMO1-dependent modification, which was associated with reduced ubiquitin-mediated degradation and enhanced ANKRD1 protein stability. Stabilized ANKRD1 subsequently promoted MERTK expression and sustained downstream AKT signaling, thereby supporting tumor cell survival under osimertinib pressure. Furthermore, K41 emerged as a critical regulatory residue, as K41R simultaneously impaired ANKRD1 SUMOylation, ubiquitination, and interaction with ZNF593, accompanied by attenuated downstream signaling and resistance phenotypes. These findings suggest that K41 plays an important role in coordinating ANKRD1 post-translational regulation and its interaction with ZNF593.
DISCUSSION: Our study identifies a proteostasis-related mechanism contributing to acquired osimertinib resistance and provides mechanistic insight into the ZNF593-ANKRD1-MERTK axis in EGFR-mutant LUAD. These findings support further investigation of this regulatory axis as a potential vulnerability in osimertinib-resistant LUAD.

title: Acute myeloid leukemia following icotinib therapy for non-small cell lung cancer: a case report and literature review.
authors: Huang H, Song L, Tong F et al.
abstract: Icotinib significantly improves survival and prognosis in patients with epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-sensitive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). It is generally well-tolerated, with treatment-related myeloid neoplasm (t-MN) being a rare adverse reaction. We report a case of a 75-year-old female patient with lung adenocarcinoma (EGFR exon 21 L858R mutation) who underwent four cycles of pemetrexed combined with platinum-based chemotherapy postoperatively, followed by radiation therapy to the supraclavicular and mediastinal lymphatic drainage regions, and sequential targeted therapy with icotinib. Approximately 32 months after initiating icotinib, the patient developed severe anemia, leading to discontinuation of the drug. She was subsequently diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) and treated with a regimen of lisaftoclax combined with azacitidine; bone marrow examination after one cycle of treatment showed partial remission. The patient later experienced relapse and progression of AML and died 4 months after the AML diagnosis. We also reviewed previous cases of t-MN induced during treatment with epidermal growth factor receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs). Based on this literature review, it remains unclear whether EGFR-TKIs are independent risk factors for t-MN. This study suggests that patients with NSCLC receiving EGFR-TKIs should undergo long-term, regular monitoring of complete blood counts. Clinicians should be vigilant for the risk of t-MN in patients with persistent cytopenia and should identify such cases and intervene as early as possible.

title: [Not Available].
authors: Ardizzoni A, Attili I, Cappuzzo F et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION:: Osimertinib has become a key therapeutic option across multiple disease settings in epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR)-mutated non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), supported by evidence from the AURA3, FLAURA, ADAURA, FLAURA2, and LAURA trials. However, uncertainties remain regarding its impact on quality of life (QoL), tolerability, and positioning as standard of care in clinical practice. This study assessed agreement among Italian experts on the role of osimertinib across the therapeutic continuum of EGFR-mutated NSCLC using a Delphi consensus methodology.
METHODS:: An 11-member Steering Committee developed and validated 35 statements covering four domains: standard of care, QoL, treatment manageability and adverse event management. The statements were evaluated through a two-round Delphi survey by an Italian Expert Panel of 28 clinicians experienced in managing EGFR-mutated NSCLC. Consensus was defined as ≥ 70% agreement (Likert scores 4-5).
RESULTS:: Among the initial 26 statements, the completion rate was 100% across both rounds, with consensus achieved for all statements. For the additional 9 statements, the completion rate was 89.3%, and consensus was again reached for all statements. High agreement supported osimertinib as a standard therapeutic option in advanced, adjuvant and unresectable stage III EGFR-mutated NSCLC. Experts also recognized its favorable impact on central nervous system disease control, QoL, treatment tolerability and long-term clinical manageability.
CONCLUSION:: This Italian Delphi Consensus confirms broad expert agreement on the central role of osimertinib across the therapeutic continuum of EGFR-mutated NSCLC, supporting its use as a standard of care in multiple clinical settings.

title: MRAS, SHOC2, PP1C and YAP1 mRNA level variations at 72 hours of targeted therapy in KRAS G12C-mutant non-small cell lung cancer cell lines.
authors: Giménez-Capitán A, Olmo-González D, Martínez-Pérez E et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The treatment of KRAS G12C-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) has become a dominant field of ongoing translational research. Still, the effect of the first KRAS G12C inhibitor, sotorasib, or next-generation inhibitors, such as fulzerasib, in KRAS-mutant NSCLC patients is short-lived. Although the objective response rate is encouraging, the median progression-free survival is 12.5 months with fulzerasib combined with cetuximab (an EGFR monoclonal antibody), and treatment efficacy is reduced when TP53, STK11, or KEAP1 mutations co-exist. In KRAS G12C sensitive cell lines, such as NCI-H358, early up regulation of MRAS and YAP1 occurs following therapy with sotorasib. We aim to assess variations in the mRNA levels of the MRAS-SHOC2-PP1C complex components that are associated with MAPK reactivation, as well as those of related genes, chiefly HUWE1 and VCP1, and among others, YAP1, the wild-type RAS isoforms HRAS and NRAS, MET, and ERFFI1, a negative regulator of EGFR.
METHODS: NCI-H358, H23, and H2030 were treated with either sotorasib or fulzerasib and in combination with cetuximab. RNA isolation was performed and NCounter and Digital Analyzer (NanoString Technologies) was used targeting 21 transcripts from gene expression analysis (MET; KRAS; MRAS, SHOC2, PP1C, HUWE1, VCP1, LIFR, SCRIBBLE, ZDHCC7, YES, YAP1, E-cadherin, FASN, LZTR1, NFE2L2, ENO1, RGS3, NRAS and HRAS). The assessment was performed at baseline and 72 hours after each treatment: Comparisons between groups were conducted using the Kruskal-Wallis and paired comparison with t-test. Student's t-test was used to calculate P values for gene expression analysis.
RESULTS: For the sensitive NCI-H358, significant upregulation of MRAS, SHOC2, PP1C, YAP1, as well as HUWE1 and VCP1, was observed after 72 hours of treatment with sotorasib and cetuximab. Either sotorasib or fulzerasib, in combination with cetuximab, upregulate ERFFI1. In the less sensitive H23, PP1C, HRAS, and MET were the most significantly overexpressed genes after 72 hours of treatment. In the resistant H2030 cell line, MRAS mRNA levels were upregulated with either sotorasib or fulzerasib or in combination with cetuximab. YAP1 was detected to be phosphorylated at Y357 by Western blot analysis.
CONCLUSIONS: The RAS pathway can be reactivated by MRAS, SHOC2, PP1C, and YAP1. Although cetuximab can upregulate ERFFI1 in NCI-H358 cells, the elevation of such transcripts warrants further investigation to determine whether to target individual components of the MRAS-SHOC2-PP1C complex or YAP1. MET mRNA levels could also be examined to identify KRAS G12C-mutant tumors in which MET may be upregulated. The effects of STK11 and/or KEAP1 co-mutations require further research.

title: Noninvasive prediction of classic EGFR-activating mutations in non-small cell lung cancer using a combined spectral computed tomography model: an auxiliary tool for preoperative stratification of candidates for EGFR-TKI therapy.
authors: Zhan Q, Lin H, Lin D et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: EGFR genotyping is essential for EGFR-TKI therapy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), but invasive biopsy has limitations. Noninvasive preoperative stratification tools are urgently needed.
METHODS: We retrospectively enrolled 129 NSCLC patients to develop and internally validate a combined model integrating clinical features, conventional CT findings, and dual-layer spectral CT parameters for predicting classic EGFR-activating mutations. Performance was evaluated by ROC, DeLong test, DCA, and 1000-iteration bootstrap validation.
RESULTS: The combined model achieved an AUC of 0.805, significantly outperforming the clinical-conventional CT model (AUC = 0.642, P < 0.001). Venous-phase normalized iodine concentration (NIC) was the only independent predictor (OR = 2.578, P = 0.018). The model showed robust performance in the lung adenocarcinoma subgroup (AUC = 0.810) with negligible overfitting.
CONCLUSIONS: This noninvasive spectral CT model provides a reliable, easy-to-implement auxiliary tool for preoperative EGFR mutation stratification to optimize EGFR-TKI therapy decisions.

title: Protocol of a Real-World Prospective Observational Study of Amivantamab Plus Chemotherapy in Patients With EGFR Exon 20 Insertion-Positive Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (SPIRAL-RACER20 Study).
authors: Sawada R, Yamada T, Shimose T et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: The PAPILLON trial demonstrated that amivantamab plus carboplatin and pemetrexed was superior to chemotherapy alone in treatment-naive patients with epidermal growth factor receptor exon 20 insertion-positive non-small cell lung cancer (EGFR exon 20 insertion-positive NSCLC). However, a substantial proportion of patients encountered in routine practice would not meet the eligibility criteria of pivotal clinical trials. Consequently, the effectiveness and safety of this regimen remain insufficiently characterized under real-world conditions, especially among Japanese patients. This study was designed to assess the effectiveness and safety of amivantamab plus chemotherapy in routine clinical practice and to explore biomarkers associated with treatment efficacy and prognosis in patients with EGFR exon 20 insertion-positive NSCLC.
METHODS: SPIRAL-RACER20 is a multicenter, prospective, noninterventional observational study enrolling patients with advanced or recurrent EGFR exon 20 insertion-positive NSCLC who are scheduled to receive amivantamab plus carboplatin and pemetrexed as part of routine clinical care. The primary endpoint is the 1-year progression-free survival (PFS) rate, while secondary endpoints include median PFS, objective response rate (ORR), time to treatment failure (TTF), safety profile, and the real-world management of dermatologic toxicities. Exploratory biomarker analyses will be conducted using blood-based next-generation sequencing (NGS) before treatment and at treatment discontinuation or completion in patients who provide consent.
DISCUSSION: This study will generate prospective real-world evidence on amivantamab-based therapy in patient populations underrepresented in registration trials.
TRIAL REGISTRATION: JAPAN REGISTRY OF CLINICAL TRIALS, JRCT1071250104; REGISTERED 28 NOVEMBER 2025.

title: ENPP1 inhibits the cGAS-STING pathway to mediate immune evasion in EGFR-TKI-resistant non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Zhou C, Liu Y, Liu H et al.
abstract: Third-generation EGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors (TKIs), such as osimertinib, have demonstrated promising clinical efficacy in the treatment of EGFR-mutant non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Despite substantial progress with EGFR-TKIs, the development of acquired resistance remains a major clinical challenge. Notably, the addition of immune checkpoint blockade after TKI resistance has not resulted in significant survival benefits compared to chemotherapy. In this study, we performed a comprehensive transcriptomic analysis of established osimertinib-resistant tumor models and found that the expression of the ectonucleotide phosphodiesterase ENPP1, a key regulator of extracellular cGAMP signaling, was significantly upregulated in resistant tumors compared to the parental TKI-sensitive NSCLC tumors. Mechanistically, upregulated ENPP1 in resistant cells promoted the hydrolysis of extracellular cGAMP, suppressing the cGAS-STING pathway in immune cells and subsequently impairing immune cell activation and function, thereby promoting immune suppression and tumor progression. Genetic depletion or pharmacological inhibition of ENPP1 enhanced immune cell-mediated cytotoxicity against TKI-resistant tumor cells. Furthermore, the use of ENPP1 inhibitors both in vitro and in vivo enhanced immune cell activity and antitumor efficacy in TKI-resistant lung cancers with high ENPP1 expression. Importantly, these observations were further validated by paired clinical tumor samples, which demonstrated increased ENPP1 expression following the development of acquired EGFR-TKI resistance. Collectively, our study highlights a critical role for ENPP1 in mediating immune evasion through suppression of the cGAMP-STING pathway in the tumor immune microenvironment, supporting ENPP1 as a promising therapeutic target to enhance immunotherapy efficacy in EGFR-TKI-resistant NSCLC.

title: Role of KCTD5 in non-small cell lung cancer progression and reduction of osimertinib sensitivity.
authors: Jiang X, Guan J, Li Q et al.
journal: Biochim Biophys Acta Mol Basis Dis
abstract: Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is the most common type of lung cancer. Here, we investigated the role of potassium channel tetramerization domain containing 5 (KCTD5), a component of Cullin3-RING E3 ubiquitin ligase complex, in NSCLC. The database analysis showed high expression levels of KCTD5 in NSCLC and its association with poor prognosis in patients with NSCLC. In vitro, KCTD5 overexpression induced cell proliferation, colony formation, and migration in NSCLC cell lines. In vivo, nude mice injected with KCTD5-overexpressing cells developed large-sized subcutaneous tumors compared to the controls. Using co-immunoprecipitation experiments, we demonstrated that KCTD5 interacted with PTEN, leading to PTEN ubiquitination and degradation. Furthermore, KCTD5 overexpression reduced H1975 cell sensitivity to osimertinib, a tyrosine kinase inhibitor. Our results indicate that KCTD5 induces NSCLC cell proliferation and migration via PTEN ubiquitination and reduced drug sensitivity of cells to osimertinib through the PTEN/AKT signaling pathway.

title: [Two Cases of Heart Failure Caused by Osimertinib].
authors: Bamba H, Kato A, Igarashi Y et al.
abstract: In recent years, an association between osimertinib and heart failure has been reported. Here, we describe 2 cases of heart failure suspected to be related to osimertinib. Case 1: An 82-year-old woman with a history of hypertension developed heart failure 16 months after starting osimertinib treatment for right upper lobe lung adenocarcinoma. Case 2: A 66-year-old man with a history of supraventricular tachycardia developed dyspnea due to tachycardia 1 month after initiating osimertinib for right lower lobe lung adenocarcinoma. Six months later, during hospitalization for arrhythmia management, his cardiac function was also found to have declined. In both cases, cardiac function improved after osimertinib was discontinued and heart failure medications were initiated.

title: Detection of Actionable Genomic Alterations beyond EGFR, ALK and ROS1 in Non-Small Cell Lung Carcinoma: A Real-World Evaluation of a Pathology-Led Staggered Reflex Predictive Biomarker Testing Strategy in a Resource-Limited Setting.
authors: Nambirajan A, Yadav K, Sahu S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Comprehensive genomic profiling is increasingly recognized as the standard for predictive biomarker testing in non-small cell lung carcinoma (NSCLC). However, resource-constrained settings face challenges with universal upfront next-generation sequencing (NGS) because of limitations in infrastructure, cost, tissue adequacy, and turnaround time.
AIMS: To assess the feasibility, diagnostic yield, and limitations of a staggered reflex biomarker testing workflow integrating single-gene testing (SGT) and targeted NGS.
METHODS: This retrospective audit included consecutive treatment-naïve NSCLC patients from March 2025 to March 2026. Samples with tumor fraction < 20% underwent SGT only, whereas those with tumor fraction ≥ 20% underwent SGT followed by targeted 40-gene DNA/RNA NGS if negative for EGFR, ALK, and ROS1. Diagnostic yield, testing attrition, and actionable genomic alterations were evaluated.
RESULTS: Of 867 patient samples, 534 (61.6%) entered the staggered workflow. SGT identified EGFR, ALK, or ROS1 alterations in 172 (32.2%). Among 362 triple-negative cases, 127 (35.1%) failed pre-library DNA and/or RNA quantity/quality requirements, and 235 (64.9%) underwent NGS. Clinically actionable alterations beyond those detected by SGT were detected in 64/235 (27.2%) patients. Overall, clinically actionable alterations were identified in 348/867 (40.1%) patients, while tissue inadequacy or molecular testing failure prevented complete biomarker evaluation in another 348 867 (40.1%) patients. KRAS was the most frequent oncogenic driver beyond EGFR/ALK/ROS1, followed by ERBB2, MET, and RET.
CONCLUSION: NGS identified clinically actionable alterations in over one-quarter of patients negative for EGFR, ALK, and ROS1. Staggered testing is a practical strategy for integrating NGS in resource-limited settings, with SGT as a reliable fallback when NGS fails.

title: Diagnostic Yield and Safety Profile of Shape-Sensing Robotic-Assisted Bronchoscopy in Peripheral Pulmonary Nodules 8 mm or Smaller.
authors: Fernandez-Bussy S, Murillo-Torres RM, Yu Lee-Mateus A et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Lung cancer screening guidelines generally recommend imaging surveillance rather than tissue sampling for nodules measuring ≤8 mm. Evidence regarding the feasibility, diagnostic performance, and safety of tissue biopsy in this lesion size remains limited. We evaluated the diagnostic performance and safety of shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy (ssRAB) for biopsy of peripheral pulmonary nodules measuring ≤8 mm.
METHODS: We conducted a retrospective single-center study of consecutive patients who underwent ssRAB between June 2020 and December 2025 for biopsy of nodules measuring ≤8 mm on pre-procedural CT imaging. The primary outcome was strict diagnostic yield, as defined by the American Thoracic Society/American College of Chest Physicians. Secondary objectives included intermediate diagnostic yield, diagnostic distribution, procedural outcomes, and complications. Diagnostic performance according to lesion size (≤ 6 mm vs. 6.1-8 mm) was evaluated separately as a subgroup analysis.
RESULTS: A total of 195 nodules were included in the study. Median lesions diameter was seven mm (IQR 6-8). Strict diagnostic yield was 70.2% (137/195), while intermediate diagnostic yield was 77.4% (151/195). Malignancy was identified in 104 lesions (53.3%). The median ssRAB procedure time was 59 min (IQR 45-83). Pneumothorax occurred in six patients (3.3%), with chest tube placement required in two (1.1%).
DISCUSSION: Shape-sensing robotic-assisted bronchoscopy demonstrated meaningful diagnostic performance and a favorable safety profile for peripheral pulmonary nodules measuring ≤8 mm, including lesions ≤6 mm. In this selected, higher-risk cohort, our findings suggest that earlier tissue diagnosis can be feasible and may benefit some patients.

title: Pharmacotherapy for older adults with cancer: a digest of the Japanese clinical practice guidelines (2nd edition) - lung cancer.
authors: Kubo T, Shimokata T, Tsukita Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The number of older adults with lung cancer is increasing in aging societies. However, determining optimal pharmacotherapy remains challenging because of heterogeneity in functional status, comorbidities, and the limited representation of older adults in clinical trials.
METHODS: This article presents an English digest of the second edition of the Japanese Clinical Practice Guidelines for Pharmacotherapy in Older Adults with Cancer, focusing on lung cancer. The guidelines were developed using the Minds 2020 methodology and incorporated systematic reviews, an evidence-to-decision framework, and multidisciplinary expert consensus.
RESULTS: These guidelines address key clinical questions in small-cell lung cancer (SCLC) and non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), including prophylactic cranial irradiation, adjuvant therapy, and immune checkpoint inhibitor-based treatments. Most recommendations were conditional, and no recommendation could be made for several clinical questions because of limited evidence in older populations. Prophylactic cranial irradiation may reduce brain metastases in selected patients with SCLC but requires careful consideration of potential neurocognitive toxicity. In resected NSCLC, tegafur-uracil may be an option for selected older patients; however, evidence supporting platinum-based chemotherapy and immunotherapy remains insufficient. In advanced NSCLC, immune checkpoint inhibitor monotherapy may benefit selected patients, whereas the role of chemoimmunotherapy remains uncertain because of insufficient age-specific evidence.
CONCLUSIONS: These guidelines provide practical, evidence-based recommendations for pharmacotherapy in older adults with lung cancer. They emphasize individualized treatment strategies based on patient characteristics, treatment goals, and tolerability. Further research in older populations is required to strengthen the evidence base for geriatric oncology.

title: From Stated Preferences to Sustained Participation in Low-Dose Computed Tomography Lung Cancer Screening: A Stage-Resolved Narrative Review.
authors: Ding T, Zhang G, Wang Y et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Low-dose computed tomography lung cancer screening (LDCT-LCS) reduces lung cancer mortality among eligible high-risk adults, yet sustained participation remains challenging. Existing studies frequently combine stated willingness, screening decisions, initial completion, and repeated participation as a single outcome or summarize determinants as undifferentiated barriers. A clearer understanding of how patient preferences translate into screening behaviors across successive stages of the screening pathway is needed.
METHODS: This narrative review was informed by searches of PubMed, Web of Science Core Collection, and Scopus conducted on August 30, 2026, with a targeted PubMed and Crossref update on September 1, 2026. Evidence was organized across five analytical domains: stated preferences, screening intention, decision, initial uptake, and rescreening and sustained participation. Study designs, outcome ascertainment, and study-level limitations informed the synthesis.
RESULTS: Patients value screening outcomes and service attributes, including cost, location, invitation processes, appointment arrangements, and navigation. Few studies link stated preferences to subsequent screening events in the same individuals. Randomized multicomponent navigation interventions improved initial uptake in the studied settings, while one factorial trial found that coordinated clinician and patient reminders improved a single 9-15-month return. Observational and qualitative studies identify access, communication, beliefs, and screening experiences associated with participation. Direct longitudinal evidence for preference-to-multiround participation remains limited.
CONCLUSION: A stage-resolved approach distinguishes preference elicitation, intention, decision quality, verified completion, and longitudinal participation. The fifth domain encompasses the first recommended rescreening and sustained participation across multiple eligible rounds. Patient-centered screening combines informed decisions with feasible implementation and longitudinal support. The framework accommodates reconsideration, informed discontinuation, and re-entry across the screening pathway.

title: Multi-scale computational analysis of MMP9 and SIRT1 regulatory networks and their interaction with curcumin and resveratrol in lung adenocarcinoma.
authors: Sheikh MR, Parvez MAS, Tasnim J et al.
abstract:
UNLABELLED: Lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) is a major cause of cancer-related morbidity and mortality, highlighting the need for therapeutic strategies capable of targeting multiple oncogenic pathways. In this study, an integrative computational framework that combines pharmacokinetic profiling, protein interaction network analysis, molecular docking, 200 ns molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, MM-GBSA binding free-energy estimation, transcriptomic analysis, genomic alteration assessment, and consensus miRNA modeling was used to explore curcumin and resveratrol as potential modulators of the molecular processes associated with MMP9 and SIRT1 in LUAD. Both compounds exhibited favorable drug-likeness characteristics, gastrointestinal absorption, and predicted low acute toxicity. Network analysis identified MMP9- and SIRT1-centered interaction networks with TP53 emerging as a common central node. Molecular docking predicted favorable interactions of curcumin with MMP9 and resveratrol with SIRT1. However, SIRT1 docking validation produced an RMSD of 2.26 Å, slightly exceeding the predefined 2.0 Å threshold; therefore, the resveratrol-SIRT1 docking result was considered supportive rather than fully validated structural evidence. The 200 ns MD simulations indicated satisfied conformational behavior of both protein-ligand complexes, supported by RMSD, hydrogen-bond, and other structural analyses. Further, MM-GBSA analysis provided complementary computational evidence for favorable binding energetics. The weak negative co-expression of both genes was observed in TCGA-LUAD analysis (P < 0.05), and they also had significant tumor-associated upregulation. The functional enrichment analysis indicated that MMP9 and SIRT1 have different but complementary roles; MMP9 was enriched with genes involved in extracellular matrix remodeling, inflammation and proteolytic processes while SIRT1 was enriched with genes involved in metabolic, epigenetic and cellular stress response processes. Importantly, the present study does not establish pharmacological synergy between curcumin and resveratrol. Instead, the synthesized results offer a hypothesis-driven approach for exploring other mechanisms potentially involving MMP9 and SIRT1 and evaluating their synergistic benefits in LUAD when combined with these two natural compounds. Experimental biochemical, cellular, pharmacokinetic, toxicological, and in vivo studies are required to validate the predicted interactions and determine their biological and therapeutic relevance.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s40203-026-00780-8.

title: Lung Cancer Screening Recommendations in the Elderly: International Society for Geriatric Oncology Consensus Statement.
authors: Steimer D, Frain L, DuMontier C et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Current or former smokers with a 20-pack-year history between the ages of 50 and 80 years are eligible for lung cancer screening (LCS) under current guidelines. Despite age restrictions for screening, older patients remain at risk for lung cancer and, without screening, are diagnosed with advanced-stage disease that limits curative treatment options.Treatment for early-stage lung cancer has improved with minimally invasive surgical techniques and reduced toxicity associated with stereotactic body radiation therapy. Robust older patients can tolerate surgical resection or stereotactic body radiation therapy with rates of recovery similar to those of their younger peers. Given the advancements in treatment and the improved tools available to identify frailty, chronological age should not be a gatekeeper for LCS.
METHODS: A taskforce within the International Society of Geriatric Oncology was created to address challenges of LCS within older patients. Taskforce members represented five different specialties with clinical expertise in lung cancer and the care of older adults.
RESULTS: For patients above 80 years old who qualify for LCS, we recommend performing a geriatric assessment (GA) to assess functional status and age-related vulnerabilities. Robust patients, as determined by GA, should be eligible for screening and discuss their health care priorities in shared decision-making conversations. GA should be performed every 2 years while patients are enrolled in LCS to determine the appropriateness of continued screening efforts.
CONCLUSIONS: Age should not be an exclusion criterion for LCS. Patients above 80 years old should be thoughtfully co-managed by geriatric and lung cancer specialists to determine which older patients would benefit from screening efforts.

title: Efficacy and safety of intrathecal chemotherapy in leptomeningeal disease: a global retrospective multicenter analysis and review of the literature.
authors: Msherghi A, Patel CB, Gule-Monroe M et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Leptomeningeal disease (LMD) is a devastating complication of cancer with limited therapeutic options and poor prognosis. It affects approximately 5-15% of patients with solid or hematopoietic malignancies. The optimal route of chemotherapy delivery for LMD patients remains controversial, with intrathecal administration theoretically offering direct access to the central nervous system. The effectiveness and safety of intrathecal chemotherapy (ITC) remain contentious, and most previous studies have been limited to small sample sizes. We aimed to assess the efficacy and safety of ITC in LMD patients using global data.
METHODS: This was a retrospective cohort study using electronic health record data from the International Collaborative TriNetX Network, comparing outcomes among patients with LMD across cancer types who received ITC plus systemic chemotherapy versus systemic chemotherapy alone. The study included all cancer types across 106 healthcare organizations, encompassing more than 156 million patients. The analysis was conducted on August 12, 2025, and eligible index events were restricted by the TriNetX platform to the preceding 20 years (August 12, 2005, through August 12, 2025). After including all cancer patients with LMD of both sexes aged between 18 and 90 years, we first excluded patients who received radiotherapy to the central nervous system. Second, 2311 subjects who received systemic chemotherapy alone and 292 subjects who received ITC plus systemic chemotherapy were included and compared using multivariate Cox regression to calculate hazard ratios (HRs). Third, propensity score matching (PSM) was performed using age, sex, primary cancer type, treatment interventions, and baseline laboratory values at diagnosis. This yielded 247 cases in each cohort, which were compared using univariate survival analysis with HRs. The primary outcome of both the univariate and multivariate analyses was all-cause mortality at multiple time points. Secondary outcomes included chemotherapy-related adverse effects, meningitis, hydrocephalus, cognitive-communication deficits, seizures, sepsis, and hypotension following treatment. A subanalysis was also performed to assess the isolated efficacy and safety of specific ITCs (in combination with systemic chemotherapy), such as methotrexate and cytarabine, compared with systemic chemotherapy alone. Finally, we conducted a literature review from inception through December 2025 to identify all prospective phase 2 and 3 clinical trials that evaluated the efficacy and safety of ITC in patients with LMD.
FINDINGS: We found that the predominant cases receiving ITC were of hematopoietic and lymphoid origin (176 patients; 71.3% in ITC vs. 173; 70% in controls), followed by breast, lung, and melanoma primary cancers (48 [19.4%], 21 [8.5%], and 17 [6.9%] in ITC vs. 59 [23.9%], 20 [8.1%], and 14 [5.7%], respectively). Multivariate Cox regression analysis revealed a significant reduction in 30-day mortality associated with ITC (HR 0.45, 95% CI 0.26-0.76; p = 0.003). At 90 days, the association with mortality did not reach statistical significance (HR = 0.75; 95% CI, 0.55-1.02; p = 0.066). By 180 days, mortality rates did not differ between cohorts (HR = 0.93; 95% CI, 0.73-1.20; p = 0.58). One-year univariate survival analysis post-PSM indicated worse survival with ITC (HR = 1.34; 95% CI, 1.01-1.78; p = 0.04). Over the follow-up period, patients receiving ITC experienced higher rates of adverse events, including meningitis (36.8% vs. 21.5%; HR 1.94; p < 0.001), hydrocephalus at 30 days (8.5% vs. 4.0%; HR 3.04; p = 0.01), and cognitive communication deficits (26.3% vs. 16.2%; HR 1.75; p = 0.01).
INTERPRETATION: This large-scale study provides important insights into the role of ITC in both solid and hematologic malignancies. Although the overall findings did not demonstrate a long-term survival benefit, ITC was associated with improved 30-day survival (HR = 0.4; p < 0.05). No difference was observed at 90 days, and beyond that time, an inverse effect emerged, possibly reflecting treatment-related toxicities and cancer-related complications. Given that survival in LMD typically ranges from 4 to 16 weeks and rarely exceeds 6 months, these results suggest that ITC provides a short-term survival advantage but may not alter, or may worsen, longer-term outcomes with a significant increase in chemotherapy adverse events, hydrocephalus, meningitis, and communicative cognitive impairment.
FUNDING: None.

title: Perioperative tislelizumab plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy for patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer: patient-reported outcomes in the RATIONALE-315 trial.
authors: Yue D, Cappuzzo F, Wang W et al.
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: In the phase III RATIONALE-315 trial (NCT04379635), perioperative tislelizumab plus neoadjuvant chemotherapy significantly improved overall and event-free survival versus placebo plus chemotherapy in patients with resectable stage II-IIIA non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Here, report prespecified patient-reported outcomes (PROs).
METHODS: PROs were evaluated using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-LC13 questionnaires. A mixed-effects model for repeated measures was used for PRO endpoints at neoadjuvant Cycle 3 and adjuvant Cycles 3, 5, and 7. Time to deterioration (TTD) was also analyzed.
RESULTS: 453 patients were randomized to tislelizumab (n = 226) or placebo (n = 227). At adjuvant Cycles 3 and 5, chest pain was maintained with tislelizumab versus worsening with placebo (LSM difference -4.99 [95% CI: -9.06 to -0.93]; p = 0.016) and -4.15 [95% CI: -7.86 to -0.44]; p = 0.028, respectively). At adjuvant Cycle 7, greater improvement in coughing was observed in the tislelizumab arm versus placebo (-5.10 [95% CI: -9.79 to -0.40]; p = 0.034). TTD analysis showed a lower risk of chest pain with tislelizumab (HR 0.58; p = 0.004).
CONCLUSION: Perioperative tislelizumab improved coughing and chest pain compared with placebo in patients with resectable NSCLC. These data provide additional support of this regimen in this patient population.
CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION: www.clinicaltrials.gov identifier is NCT04379635.

title: ParetoRx: A Multiobjective Radiogenomic Framework Integrating Pareto Optimization and Q-Learning for Exploratory Compound Prioritization in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer.
authors: Kawahara D, Kishi M, Kadooka Y
abstract: Imaging-defined high-risk phenotypes may capture biologically aggressive disease states, but translating them into therapeutic hypotheses remains challenging. We developed ParetoRx, a radiogenomic imaging-informatics framework integrating computed tomography radiomics, pathway-level transcriptomic analysis, multiobjective Pareto optimization, and model-free Q-learning for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Pretreatment CT data from 402 patients were used for model development and internal validation, with 110 patients forming a held-out external cohort. The final radiomics model achieved an external C-index of 0.707 (95% CI 0.627-0.783); high-risk patients had worse overall survival (HR 3.461, 95% CI 1.674-7.153), with minimal change after adjustment for histology (HR 3.444, 95% CI 1.662-7.137). Gene set enrichment and single-sample pathway analyses identified exploratory associations involving E2F targets, MYC targets V1, inflammatory response, and hypoxia, although no pathway met FDR < 0.05. LINCS L1000 perturbational profiles were evaluated using transcriptomic reversal, pathway specificity, and a feasibility-related proxy, with 4188 compounds retained in the common complete-case analysis. Multiobjective Pareto optimization was combined with three-split consensus ranking and sequential policy evaluation. TWS-119 showed consistent prioritization across all three splits (ranks 1, 3, and 4) and was Pareto-optimal in each split. In simulation-based evaluation, model-free Q-learning achieved higher terminal-goal attainment than myopic and static policies across all three splits, with improvements of approximately 6.2-13.3 percentage points over the myopic comparator. These findings support ParetoRx as an exploratory framework for biologically informed compound prioritization and computational sequential decision-making, while independent drug response and clinical validation remain necessary.

title: Soxataltinib, a highly selective CNS-penetrant RET inhibitor demonstrates durable activity in RET fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer phase 2 study.
authors: Xiong A, Meng X, Li X et al.
abstract: Selective RET inhibitors have transformed the treatment landscape of RET fusion-positive non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), yet durable systemic and intracranial disease control remains a major clinical challenge. We conducted a multicenter, single-arm phase 2 study of soxataltinib, a highly selective CNS-penetrant RET inhibitor, in treatment-naïve (n=56) and previously treated patients (n=49) with advanced RET fusion-positive NSCLC. At a median follow-up of 19.3 months, the independent review committee (IRC)-assessed ORR was 84.8% (95% CI, 76.4-91.0), including 89.3% in treatment-naïve and 79.6% in previously treated patients. Responses were observed across clinically relevant subgroups, including patients with baseline brain metastases. Median progression-free survival (PFS) was not reached in the overall population. Intracranial response was observed in patients with measurable CNS disease [ intracranial ORRs were 100% (4/4) in treatment-naïve and 60.0% (3/5) in previously treated patients], supporting clinically meaningful CNS control. Grade ≥3 TRAEs occurred in 76.2% of patients and were generally manageable with dose modification; treatment discontinuation due to adverse events occurred in 1.9%, with no treatment-related deaths. Soxataltinib demonstrated durable systemic and intracranial antitumor activity in RET fusion-positive NSCLC, supporting its further development as a next-generation RET-targeted therapy.

title: Adverse events in placebo arms of phase III lung cancer trials: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
authors: Zhang J, Chen W, Mi L et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Adverse events (AEs) are routinely reported in placebo arms of lung cancer trials, yet these data have seldom been systematically synthesized. This meta-analysis aimed to quantify the incidence of AEs in placebo arms of phase III randomized controlled trials (RCTs) for non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) and small cell lung cancer (SCLC).
METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Ovid Medline, and Cochrane Library for phase III RCTs evaluating targeted therapy and/or immunotherapy in NSCLC or SCLC that included a placebo arm. Pooled incidence was estimated using random-effects models for any-grade and grade 3 or 4 AEs, treatment modifications (interruption, dose reduction, or discontinuation) due to AEs, and common AEs.
RESULTS: Twenty-six RCTs comprising 7641 placebo-treated patients were included. The pooled incidence of any-grade AEs was 84% (95%CI: 78-90%, 95%PI: 54-100%), with grade 3 or 4 AEs occurring in 25% (95%CI: 19-32%, 95%PI: 4-57%). The most frequent any-grade AEs were fatigue (20%), dyspnea (20%), and cough (20%). Grade 3 or 4 AEs most commonly included fatigue (4%), dyspnea (3%), pneumonia (2%), and hypertension (2%). Treatment interruption or dose reduction due to AEs occurred in 10% (95%CI: 6-15%, 95%PI: 0-36%), and discontinuation in 5% (95%CI: 4-8%, 95%PI: 0-17%).
CONCLUSION: Placebo-treated patients with lung cancer experience substantial AE burden, may attributable to disease itself and its prior treatment. The scarcity of nocebo-related data underscores the urgent need for future studies to investigate its mechanisms and systematically assess negative expectancy in patients.
