title: Superior Vena Cava Syndrome and Pulmonary Embolism Revealing a Lung Sarcomatoid Carcinoma: An Uncommon Presentation of a Rare Tumor.
authors: Chadli A, Berhili S, BenSghier A et al.
abstract: Pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma (PSC) is a rare and highly aggressive subtype of non-small cell lung cancer, associated with early metastatic spread and poor prognosis. Tumor-related thromboembolic complications and superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome are uncommon but severe manifestations. We report the case of a 62-year-old man with a history of smoking and alcohol use, presenting with a large right upper lobe tumor with widespread metastases, associated with radiologically suspected tumor-related pulmonary embolism and SVC invasion with multiple venous thromboses. Bronchoscopic biopsy with immunohistochemical analysis confirmed PSC. The patient received anticoagulation and urgent palliative radiotherapy (20 Gy in five fractions) for brain metastases and SVC syndrome. This case highlights the aggressive nature of PSC, its association with rare vascular complications, and the challenges of emergency palliative management in patients with advanced disseminated disease.

title: Unexpected Acute Pancreatitis After Tarlatamab in Small Cell Lung Cancer: A Case Report.
authors: Anyadibe A, Amjad S, Onyechi E et al.
abstract: Tarlatamab is a bispecific T-cell engager (BiTE) targeting delta-like ligand 3, recently approved for relapsed extensive-stage small cell lung cancer. Its toxicity profile is primarily characterized by cytokine release syndrome and neurotoxicity. Pancreatitis has not been well described. We report a case of acute pancreatitis occurring approximately eight hours after the first dose, followed by completion of subsequent scheduled doses without recurrence. A 62-year-old man developed severe epigastric pain on cycle 1, day 1, after receiving tarlatamab. Lipase was elevated, and imaging confirmed acute interstitial pancreatitis. There was no history of alcohol use, and evaluation did not demonstrate gallstones, biliary obstruction, hypertriglyceridemia, hypercalcemia, or autoimmune disease. The patient improved with supportive care. After recovery, he proceeded with the remaining scheduled doses of cycle 1, which were completed without recurrence of symptoms. This case highlights a possible early, transient pancreatic toxicity and suggests that treatment may be completed in selected patients after resolution of symptoms.

title: Work productivity impairment and its associated factors among patients with cancer in Bangladesh: a hospital-based cross-sectional study.
authors: Mothashin M, Khatun R, Hossain MT et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cancer imposes substantial physical, psychosocial, and economic burdens on affected individuals, particularly in low- and middle-income countries where out-of-pocket healthcare financing remains dominant. Despite these challenges, evidence on work productivity impairment among patients with cancer in Bangladesh is limited. This study aimed to evaluate work productivity impairment and identify the factors associated with it among cancer patients in Bangladesh.
METHODS: A hospital-based cross-sectional study was conducted among 300 patients with cancer receiving treatment or follow-up care at two tertiary-level hospitals in Bangladesh: Rajshahi Medical College Hospital and Faridpur Medical College Hospital. Work productivity impairment was assessed using the validated Work Productivity and Activity Impairment (WPAI) questionnaire, with overall work impairment derived from absenteeism and presenteeism scores. Descriptive statistics were used to summarize participants' characteristics and work productivity outcomes, while beta regression analysis was performed to identify factors associated with overall work impairment.
RESULTS: The mean absenteeism, presenteeism, and overall work impairment scores were 38.1%, 49.7%, and 63.3%, respectively. Overall, work productivity impairment was substantial, with presenteeism contributing more to productivity loss than absenteeism. Beta regression analysis showed that older age (β = 0.028, p < 0.001), higher levels of occupational physical activity (β = 0.032, p = 0.028), having lung cancer (β = 1.208, p < 0.001), prostate cancer (β = 1.139, p < 0.001), and other cancers comprising skin, liver, laryngeal, hematological, bone, and cervical cancers (β = 0.721, p < 0.001) compared with thyroid cancer, being diagnosed with stage II cancer (β = 0.389, p = 0.011) compared with stage I and a longer duration since diagnosis (β = 0.101, p = 0.012) were significantly associated with greater work impairment. In contrast, higher educational attainment was significantly associated with lower work impairment (β = - 0.039, p = 0.018).
CONCLUSION: Cancer patients in Bangladesh experience substantial work productivity impairment, highlighting a severe dual functional and financial burden. Both clinical and socio-demographic factors significantly influenced productivity loss. The findings underscore the urgent need for affordable cancer care, workplace accommodation policies, and strengthened financial risk protection mechanisms to reduce the economic and occupational consequences of cancer in Bangladesh.
IMPLICATIONS FOR CANCER SURVIVORS: Targeted support can help cancer survivors maintain work productivity, reduce financial hardship, and improve quality of life.

title: [Anaphylactic Shock Induced by Indocyanine Green During Right Lung Segmentectomy].
authors: Yamazaki N, Sakaguchi Y, Tanaka H et al.
abstract: A 79-year-old man underwent thoracoscopic right S6 segmentectomy for suspected lung adenocarcinoma. Indocyanine green (ICG) was intravenously administered twice to identify the intersegmental plane. Approximately 10 minutes after the second injection, profound hypotension refractory to vasopressors developed. Cutaneous flushing was subsequently observed, and intraoperative anaphylactic shock was diagnosed. Hemodynamic stability was achieved after intramuscular adrenaline administration along with antihistamines and corticosteroids. The surgery was completed without further complications, and the postoperative course was uneventful. Although ICG is generally considered safe, it can rarely cause life-threatening anaphylaxis. Under general anesthesia, early symptoms may be masked, delaying diagnosis. With the increasing use of ICG fluorescence in thoracic surgery, perioperative preparedness, prompt recognition of circulatory changes, and immediate availability of adrenaline are essential for patient safety.

title: Does Molecularly Guided Therapy Change the Surgical Goals of Glioma Resection?
authors: Haq NU, Irshad SU, Ullah I et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: For more than 20 years, the goal of glioma surgery has been to remove as much tumor as possible without compromising patient safety. Many retrospective studies support that greater extent of resection is often associated with longer survival. However, three recent developments have challenged this traditional approach. First, the 2021 World Health Organization classification introduced a molecular approach to glioma diagnosis, which made tumor biology an additional consideration, alongside imaging, in setting surgical targets. Second, the IDH-targeted therapies, particularly vorasidenib for IDH-mutant low-grade gliomas, have made residual disease a clinically meaningful variable rather than a surgical failure. Third, early phase locoregional chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell trials have suggested that the resection cavity may be an important site for treatment delivery. These developments raise a question: should the goal of glioma surgery remain the same when targeted and locoregional therapies are available? In this review, we examine the evidence for extent of resection and discuss how newer therapies may affect surgical decision-making.
METHODS: A structured literature search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science (inception to May 2026) was conducted, and evidence quality was graded narratively.
FINDINGS: We argue that these therapies do not replace maximal safe resection but reshape its application in clinical practice. Surgical planning may increasingly need to consider tissue sampling and access for future therapies alongside tumor removal. We also highlight five key controversies and outline five priorities for future research.
CONCLUSION: Based on the available evidence, we propose an oncofunctional-immunotherapeutic framework in which molecular subtype is considered before surgery, the resection cavity is seen as a potential therapeutic site, and preservation of neurological function remains essential for enabling further treatment. These elements are not yet integrated into a single clinical framework.

title: Dual‑targeting therapeutic strategies for glioblastoma (Review).
authors: Zhao Y, Xiao L, Dong Q et al.
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most aggressive primary malignant tumour, owing to intratumoural heterogeneity, adaptive resistance, and an immunosuppressive microenvironment. Dual‑targeting strategies aim to exploit complementary therapeutic vulnerabilities; however, their mechanisms of action and levels of supporting evidence vary considerably. The present narrative review evaluates single‑molecule inhibitors, dual‑antigen cellular therapies, oncolytic virus platforms, nanocarrier systems, and combination approaches directed against glioma stem‑like and differentiated cellular states or spatially distinct tumour regions. Distinctions are made between molecular co‑inhibition, dual‑antigen recognition, coordinated drug delivery, and multimodal therapeutic strategies. Evidence derived from isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH)‑mutant glioma and other malignancies is considered separately from evidence in IDH‑wildtype GBM. Vorasidenib (AG‑881) inhibits both mutant IDH1 and mutant IDH2 within the same metabolic pathway; however, its clinical benefit in grade 2 IDH‑mutant glioma does not demonstrate efficacy in GBM. Most alternative approaches remain at the preclinical stage, whereas early cellular therapy approaches have shown biological activity alongside significant limitations in response durability and neurological tolerability. Key challenges examined include clonal evolution, lineage plasticity, epigenetic and metabolic adaptation, patient stratification, and integration with radiotherapy. Translational priorities include confirming adequate drug exposure and engagement of both targets, identifying biologically appropriate patient populations, establishing tolerable treatment schedules, and streamlining manufacturing processes. Limiting tumour adaptation remains a testable therapeutic hypothesis rather than an established clinical outcome of dual targeting. Future progress will depend on research that links mechanistic complementarity to durable disease control and acceptable toxicity.

title: Nanobodies as next-generation antigen recognition domains for CAR-based cellular immunotherapies in cancer.
authors: Maali A, Fazelian S, Jafari M et al.
abstract: Nanobody-based chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) represent a promising strategy for improving the specificity, modularity, and clinical adaptability of cellular immunotherapies. Replacing conventional single-chain variable fragments with camelid-derived variable heavy-chain domains (VHHs) may enhance receptor stability, antigen accessibility, and construct design. This review summarizes nanobody-based CAR applications across T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, γδ T cells, and macrophages, drawing on literature published between 2011 and 2026 and identified through PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar. Nanobody-based CAR-T cells support recognition of hematologic and solid tumors and facilitate dual targeting, tandem receptors, affinity tuning, and immune-modulating designs. CAR-NK cells combine antigen-directed activity with innate cytotoxicity and potential advantages for allogeneic, off-the-shelf treatment. CAR-γδ T cells integrate innate-like surveillance with engineered specificity and may offer reduced graft-versus-host disease risk. CAR-macrophages exploit phagocytosis and tumor microenvironment remodeling to promote antitumor responses. Emerging universal, switchable, -generated, and synthetic antigen-based CAR platforms further highlight the versatility of nanobodies for controllable and scalable therapies. Collectively, these approaches offer opportunities to address tumor heterogeneity, antigen escape, and treatment safety, although further preclinical optimization and rigorous clinical evaluation are needed to establish their efficacy, persistence, and long-term safety in diverse patient populations and clinical settings.

title: Application of Mechanistic Modeling to Support Dose-Relevant Decision Making for CAR-T Cell Therapy in Oncology: A Systematic Scoping Review.
authors: Odujinrin D, McClelland G
abstract: CAR-T therapy has improved outcomes in selected relapsed or refractory hematologic malignancies. However, rational dose-relevant decision application remains challenging because the administered (nominal) cell dose does not reliably predict in vivo exposure, toxicity, or clinical response. These relationships are not adequately characterized by empirical dose escalation alone. Mechanistic modeling may offer a biologically interpretable way to connect preclinical evidence and patient-level CAR-T posology, but its application remains incompletely defined. We conducted a systematic scoping review using JBI methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidance, searching MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, and Google Scholar (2010-2025). Eligible studies reported original CK/PD, PK/PD, QSP, PBPK/PD, stochastic, or agent-based models for dose-relevant application or regimen optimization. Nineteen studies met the inclusion criteria (13 mechanistic and 6 semi-mechanistic models) spanning hematologic and solid-tumor settings. Although these studies evaluated aspects of CAR-T pharmacology, none provided prospectively validated clinical dose-selection evidence. Overall, CAR-T expansion appeared to be more influenced by tumor burden, antigen engagement, product-specific attributes, lymphodepletion, and host or tumor-site factors than by nominal dose. Solid-tumor models highlighted delivery route, trafficking, biodistribution, and microenvironment barriers. Emerging in vivo CAR-T platforms shifted dose considerations toward vector or mRNA dose and repeat dosing. Mechanistic modeling appears useful for framing CAR-T dose-relevant and regimen questions, but the current evidence is best interpreted as a taxonomy of model applications rather than proof of prospective clinical dose selection utility. Consistent with ICH M15 principles, future clinical, and regulatory application will require defined context of use, stronger validation, uncertainty assessment, and biological integration.

title: Emerging cell therapies for gastrointestinal cancers: Advances and future perspectives.
authors: Kanaya N, Kuroda S, Chen KS et al.
abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, including colorectal and pancreatic cancers, remain among the most lethal cancers worldwide. These tumors often exhibit resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors, largely due to microsatellite stability and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). While chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has demonstrated curative potential in hematological cancers, its translation to solid tumors has been limited by challenges such as antigen heterogeneity, physical barriers to infiltration, and TME-mediated immunosuppression. Gene-editing technologies, including CRISPR-Cas9, have catalyzed the development of next-generation cellular immunotherapies. By precisely modifying T cells, natural killer (NK) cells, and mesenchymal stem/stromal cells (MSCs), it is possible to enhance their functionality, persistence, and safety. This review highlights the clinical progress of gene-edited cell therapies and specifically explores the synergistic "one-two punch" potential of engineered MSCs as TME remodeling platforms. By acting as localized delivery vehicles for cytokines or prodrug-activating enzymes, MSCs can modulate TME, thereby facilitating the infiltration and sustained cytotoxic activity of CAR T or CAR NK cells. Finally, we address critical translational challenges and propose future directions that integrate multi-omics to identify novel therapeutic agents for cellular immunotherapy in GI oncology.

title: Mechanism-resolving development of solid-tumor CAR T-cell therapy: linking programmable control to tissue pharmacodynamics.
authors: Vo MC, Kim SK, Bae WK et al.
abstract: Solid-tumor CAR T-cell programs increasingly combine biomarker selection, lymphodepletion, manufacturing-state optimization, regional or repeated administration, and engineered control modules. This growing complexity creates a distinct translational problem: the same response, non-response, or toxicity can remain compatible with several competing explanations, obscuring which component actually operated in patient tissue. Mechanism-resolving development addresses this problem by treating each consequential engineering claim as a prospectively testable proposition embedded within the product-trial system. Four questions must be resolved: which patient-relevant state was present, which control action altered it, which proximal tissue transition followed, and which unsafe or limiting state emerged next. Each claim should therefore be paired with a clinically credible lower-burden counterfactual, mechanism-proximal tissue pharmacodynamics, a prespecified falsification criterion, a rescue strategy, and an adaptive action. Boolean coincidence and veto circuits, temporal IF-THEN systems, quantitative antigen-density filters, and genotype-conditioned activator-blocker designs require distinct representations, transition-state assays, and tissue biomarkers. Clinical evidence from CLDN18.2-directed satri-cel, compartmental central nervous system programs, hypoxia-responsive CEA therapy, GPC3-armored products, PSMA programs, and early HLA-loss-gated Tmod therapy illustrates that clinical maturity and mechanistic attribution are not equivalent. Programmability becomes translationally meaningful when the operation of an added control can be distinguished from credible alternatives in patient-relevant tissue, enabling complex cellular engineering to generate falsifiable, cumulative, and clinically actionable knowledge.

title: Evidence gaps and route-dependent development requirements for CAR cellular therapy in urothelial carcinoma: a systematic evidence map and public-data analysis.
authors: Liu J, Guo Z, Guo J et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-engineered cells are being investigated for urothelial carcinoma, but evidence requirements for antigen selection and local or systemic delivery remain undefined. We asked whether any target or route can presently be prioritised.
METHODS: We combined a systematic evidence map and registry audit with secondary analysis of public bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomes and normal-tissue resources. In GSE169379, infercnvpy used same-object non-epithelial reference cells; epithelial nuclei with high copy-number variation (CNV-high) scores were defined as those above the 99th percentile of reference scores. Aggregate rankings were replaced by two evidence gates: antigen eligibility and then product- and route-specific exposure validation. No new participants or experiments were included.
RESULTS: All 13 peer-reviewed primary studies were preclinical; none reported a treated patient with urothelial carcinoma. Five registry programmes were retained without bladder-specific results; the only urothelial-specific record changed from recruiting to terminated. Among 21,756 sampled epithelial nuclei from the 29,974-nucleus GSE169379 tumour object, 1,828 were classified CNV-high using 8,218 non-epithelial nuclei from the same object as the reference. Across 18 evaluable patients, median detection fractions were 0.083 for NECTIN4, 0.169 for ERBB2, 0.229 for CD44, 0.267 for EGFR, 0.385 for PSCA and 0.093 for MUC16; corresponding medians in four normal-urothelial batches were 0.290, 0.401, 0.423, 0.598, 0.527 and 0.008. These unpaired cross-object RNA contrasts do not establish a therapeutic window. Equal-dose intravesical MUC16-directed CAR T cells outperformed intravenous administration in two orthotopic xenograft models and showed bladder-localised exposure, but this single programme cannot establish a general route advantage or human safety.
CONCLUSIONS: No evaluated target meets requirements for unqualified clinical prioritisation. Epitope-matched malignant-cell surface expression and functional normal-tissue safety should precede testing whether a specific route achieves the exposure required by the intended disease distribution. Current route evidence is product-specific and preclinical.

title: A living enzymatic adenosine switch couples metabolic rescue to IL-12-driven antitumor immunity.
authors: Romee R, Sendker S, Yang S et al.
abstract: Cancer cells remodel their metabolic environment to disable infiltrating immune cells. Adenosine is a principal mediator of this immunosuppression, impairing the metabolism and effector functions of T and natural killer (NK) cells. Blocking adenosine receptors or production within a redundant signaling network leaves the metabolite itself intact and has shown limited clinical efficacy. Adenosine deaminase (ADA) instead converts adenosine into inosine, a metabolite that can fuel T cell metabolism. We engineered non-pathogenic, tumor-tropic Escherichia coli K-12 DH5α to surface-display ADA, confining this metabolic switch to the tumor, and co-displayed interleukin-12 (IL-12) to couple metabolic rescue to local immune stimulation. Bacteria-displayed ADA alone restored metabolic and proliferative fitness in adenosine-suppressed lymphocytes to baseline, whereas incorporation of IL-12 coupled this rescue to enhanced effector function. Across multiple preclinical models of hematologic and solid malignancies, the dual-function bacteria were well tolerated, enhanced tumor control, prolonged survival, and induced durable protective immunity against melanoma rechallenge. The bacteria were enriched at tumor sites, reactivated quiescent immune compartments in leukemia, enhanced CAR-NK cell tumor trafficking and activity in pancreatic cancer, and outperformed recombinant proteins in breast cancer. These findings establish a modular living immunotherapeutic strategy that couples a local extracellular metabolic switch with localized cytokine delivery.

title: First-in-human quad-targeting CAR T cells for diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma: a phase 1 trial.
authors: Ronsley R, Bannick M, Narayanaswamy P et al.
abstract: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) and diffuse midline glioma (DMG) are lethal pediatric central nervous system (CNS) tumors with a median survival of 11 months. Despite advancements in translating chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cells for these patients, efficacy may be constrained by antigen heterogeneity and immune escape. We conducted a first-in-human, phase 1 trial (BrainChild-04; NCT05768880) evaluating repetitive intracerebroventricular (ICV) administration of a multi-antigen targeting CAR T cell product directed against B7-H3, EGFR806, HER2 and IL13Rα2 (quad-CAR T cells) for children and young adults with DIPG/pontine DMG (Arm A) and recurrent or refractory CNS tumors (Arm B). Here we report results from Arm A. Primary endpoints were feasibility, safety, and determination of the maximally tolerated dose regimen (MTDR). Secondary endpoints included CAR T cell distribution and preliminary clinical activity. Correlative analyses assessed CAR T cell kinetics and cytokine dynamics in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Twenty-six patients were enrolled with 100% manufacturing success rate. Twenty-one patients received at least one infusion (median 8/patient, range 3-56). No dose-limiting toxicities occurred in the dose-finding period, and treatment was tolerable with predominantly grade 1-2 adverse events, including fever (95%), headache (86%), and fatigue (81%). One dose-limiting toxicity (acoustic nerve disorder) occurred outside the evaluation window. Repetitive ICV dosing was feasible, and most of the infused patients (86%) initiated two or more treatment courses (median 4). CAR T cells were detected in CSF in 100% of patients, across serial courses in 76% of patients, with evidence of detection across sequential courses, particularly at higher dose levels. Cytokine profiling demonstrated dynamic immune activation within the CNS. Median survival from initial CAR T infusion was 8.6 months (95% CI: 5.2-10.3). All deaths were due to disease progression. Repetitive ICV administration of quad-CAR T cells is feasible and tolerable in children and young adults with DIPG/DMG. This study represents the first clinical application of quad-antigen targeting CAR T cells and confirmed feasibility in manufacturing and preliminary evidence of biologic activity in the CNS. These findings support further evaluation of multi-antigen CAR T strategies to address tumor heterogeneity of antigen expression as a likely barrier to CAR T cell efficacy in patients with CNS tumors.

title: Immunotherapy in Glioblastoma: Why promising strategies fail to improve survival.
authors: Salar O, Masroor M, Chaudhary K et al.
abstract: Immunotherapy has transformed the management of several extracranial malignancies; however, its efficacy in GBM has been limited. Large clinical trials evaluating immune checkpoint inhibitors have failed to demonstrate meaningful survival benefit in newly diagnosed and recurrent GBM. Other modalities, including dendritic cell vaccines, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapies, and oncolytic virotherapy, have shown encouraging but modest results in selected patients. This narrative review summarizes the current role of immunotherapy in GBM, focussing on its impact on patient outcomes, underlying barriers to therapeutic success, and future directions.

title: Spatiotemporal control of CAR-T cell TNF release via tumor-targeted irradiation.
authors: Masoumi E, Walczak P, Tsuji T et al.
abstract: Adoptive chimeric antigen receptor (CAR)-T cell therapies have limited efficacy in solid tumors because of poor infiltration and impaired effector function, whereas radiotherapy is constrained by radioresistance and metastatic spread. Here we show that integrating the spatial precision of ionizing radiation with the biological specificity of CAR-T cells enables localized delivery of the inflammatory cytokine tumor necrosis factor (TNF). We identified radiation-responsive genes in tumor-infiltrating T cells and engineered synthetic radioinducible promoters to drive TNF expression. Human CAR-T cells carrying this construct (riTNF CAR-T cells) secreted high levels of TNF upon irradiation, independently of antigen engagement. In human xenograft and murine tumor models, the combination of riTNF CAR-T cells and local irradiation produced greater tumor regression than either treatment alone or standard CAR-T cells with irradiation. This response was associated with high intratumoral, but not systemic, TNF levels, increased tumor necrosis and apoptosis, vascular disruption and greater CAR-T cell infiltration. These findings establish a platform for spatially and temporally controlled cytokine delivery from engineered CAR-T cells.

title: Armored IL-18 CAR-T cells: bioinformatics-guided design for cold tumor infiltration.
authors: Mehmood MS, Ullah H, Wajid T et al.
abstract: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy has shown remarkable efficacy in hematologic malignancies, yet its translation to solid tumors remains a fundamental challenge. Immunologically "cold" tumors, characterized by poor T cell infiltration, dense stromal barriers, and a profoundly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME), continue to resist conventional CAR-T cell approaches. Armored CAR-T cells engineered to secrete interleukin-18 (IL-18) represent a promising fourth-generation strategy designed to overcome these limitations. IL-18 operates at the interface of innate and adaptive immunity, driving M1 macrophage polarization, dendritic cell maturation, NK cell activation, and the induction of CXCL9/CXCL10 chemokine gradients that restore lymphocyte trafficking into tumor tissue. To guide the rational design of these constructs, bioinformatics pipelines play an increasingly central role. Multi-omics integration of transcriptomic, proteomic, and single-cell RNA sequencing data enables precise tumor antigen selection, epitope prediction, and structural optimization of CAR constructs using tools such as AlphaFold, RosettaDock, and NetMHCpan. In silico safety screening further evaluates off-target toxicity risks and cross-reactivity against healthy tissues. Controlled IL-18 delivery strategies, including NFAT-inducible promoters, SynNotch logic-gated systems, and Granzyme B-cleavable pro-IL-18 constructs, provide spatial and temporal safeguards against systemic hyperinflammation. Preclinical evidence from xenograft and syngeneic models demonstrates enhanced tumor control, sustained T cell persistence, and induction of endogenous anti-tumor immunity. This review synthesizes current evidence and highlights how bioinformatics-guided engineering of IL-18 armored CAR-T cells offers a translatable framework for converting cold tumors into immunologically responsive, therapeutically tractable targets.

title: Antigen scaffolds drive preferential expansion of functional genetically engineered CAR and TCR T cells.
authors: Johansen KH, Ramanathan K, Rodriguez-Pardo C et al.
abstract: T cells engineered to express recombinant T cell receptors (TCRs) or chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) can induce durable clinical responses in solid and hematological malignancies. However, manufacturing is resource intensive and often yields highly differentiated, exhausted T cell products. To address this, we developed an antigen-scaffold (Ag-scaffold) technology that presents cognate antigen alongside stimulatory cytokines to preferentially expand genetically engineered T cells. We expanded CRISPR-Cas9- and lentivirally engineered TCR T cells with peptide MHC (pMHC)-presenting Ag-scaffolds and anti-CD19 CAR T cells with CD19-presenting Ag-scaffolds. By applying cognate pMHC Ag-scaffolds, we achieved on average 69% (±22%) antigen-specific T cells after 14 days of culture with a cytotoxic, proliferative profile. Ag-scaffold expansion enhanced initial TCR and CAR cytotoxicity; repeated rechallenges showed sustained control. In vivo, Ag-scaffold-expanded CRISPR-Cas9-engineered NY-ESO-1-specific TCR T cells and anti-CD19 CAR T cells also showed improved tumor control in lymphoma and solid tumor xenograft models compared to cells expanded with IL2/7/15.

title: Enhancing cancer immunotherapy: The role of CAR-T cells and oncolytic viruses in modulating tumor microenvironment.
authors: Shirazi N, Pashaei S, Ajam-Hosseini M et al.
abstract: Cancer immunotherapy has revolutionized oncology by improving therapeutic specificity and efficacy, leading to major clinical successes. Among these approaches, chimeric antigen receptor (CAR-T) cell therapy has shown remarkable results in hematological malignancies. However, its effectiveness in solid tumors is limited by antigen heterogeneity, poor tumor infiltration, and the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). To address these limitations, combining CAR-T therapy with oncolytic viruses (OVs) has gained increasing attention. OVs selectively infect and lyse tumor cells while simultaneously stimulating innate and adaptive antitumor immune responses through enhanced antigen release and inflammatory signaling, thereby modulating the TME and enhancing antigen presentation. Evidence from preclinical studies and early clinical trials indicates that CAR-T and OV combination therapy can generate synergistic antitumor effects by improving immune cell infiltration, enhancing cytotoxic activity, and reducing immune evasion. This review highlights recent Advances in the engineering of CAR-T cells and OVs and their synergistic potential in the treatment of solid tumors.

title: The Complex Interplay Between Cancer and the Lung Microbiome
summary: Background: The lung fosters a diverse microbiome that may have a complex interplay with underlying diseases, such as lung cancer. However, existing literature has revealed diverse results, likely owing to small sample sizes and diverse sampling methods. In this context, we aim to characterize the lung microbiome and its association with malignancy via multiple sampling methods during lung resection. Methods: Patients undergoing lung resection for confirmed malignancy were prospectively included in the study. During the operation, a bronchial swab and a parenchymal biopsy of lung tissue were collected from the resected specimen and sent for analysis via 16S rRNA gene amplicon (V4) sequencing. An established bioinformatics pipeline was used to determine taxonomic identification and compare these results to clinical and tumor data. Results: There were 83 participants included, with 75 (90.4%) patients having primary lung tumors and 8 (9.6%) having metastatic lesions. Resections included lobectomy (69.9%), wedge (25.3%), and segmentectomy (4.8%). Lung microbiome composition differed by primary malignancy site (lung vs metastatic; p=0.014) and tumor mutations (TP53, p=0.040; KRAS, p=0.054). For primary lung cancer, there was no difference in microbiome composition by tumor histology. A near-significant association was noted for patients with prolonged air leaks and alpha diversity of the lung microbiome (p=0.070). Conclusions: In this study, we demonstrate associations between the lung microbiome and underlying malignancy and tumor characteristics. Validation of these results may assist with diagnostic, prognostic, and therapeutic interventions in the operative and peri-operative management of lung cancer.

title: Clonal Hematopoiesis and Incident Solid Cancers Resolved by Histologic Subtype: A Prospective Cohort Study
summary: Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential (CHIP) is a recognized precursor of myeloid malignancy and an independent cardiovascular risk factor, but its relationship with solid tumors is incompletely defined, particularly at histologic resolution. Here, we quantify the association between CHIP and incident cancer across hematologic and solid-organ sites, by clone size, mutation number, and histologic subtype in a prospective cohort of UK Biobank participants with baseline genetic sequencing and cancer ascertained by national registry linkage; those with pre-baseline cancer were excluded. Vanderbilt BioVU was used for replication. CHIP was associated with any incident cancer (HR, 1.22; 95% CI, 1.18-1.27) and with all solid tumors combined (HR, 1.13; 95% CI, 1.08-1.19). Among 17 endpoints, two survived multiple testing correction: lung adenocarcinoma (HR, 1.79; 95% CI, 1.48 - 2.16) and esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (HR, 2.28; 95% CI, 1.37-3.81). Risk increased with clone size and multi-hit CHIP, most markedly for esophageal cancer (VAF [≥]30%: HR, 2.72), and the esophageal squamous association persisted in 5-year landmark analysis (HR, 2.57). In BioVU, CHIP was directionally associated with esophageal cancer and lung adenocarcinoma and its association with all solid tumors overall (HR, 1.24; 95% CI, 1.17-1.32) was confirmed. These findings extend CHIP from a hematologic and cardiovascular risk marker to a risk marker of solid-organ cancer risk with histologic resolution and motivate clone-size aware risk models and mechanistic studies.

title: A lactate-mitochondrial axis framework for mild hyperthermia and checkpoint blockade in driver-negative NSCLC: testing temporal coupling.
authors: Liu M, Song Y, Zhang H et al.
abstract: Metabolic constraints, including hypoxia, lactate, and adenosine that impair CD8+ T-cell function and mitochondrial fitness, are increasingly recognized as contributors to resistance to immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) in driver-negative (lacking an established first-line actionable driver alteration) advanced non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). We propose a hypothesis-driven framework asking whether transient tissue-level metabolic relief can be temporally aligned with the slower process of T-cell reinvigoration driven by immune checkpoint blockade (ICB). Its mechanistic basis is a lactate-mitochondrial axis linking extracellular metabolic suppression to mitochondrial states in tumor-infiltrating T cells, with T-cell-intrinsic mitochondrial adaptation treated as a testable extension. Locoregional mild hyperthermia (39-42 °C) is conceptualized as a transient modulator of tissue-level metabolic gradients rather than a direct immune activator. Because oxygenation, metabolite distribution, and acid-base status may change independently or in opposing directions, oxygenation is treated as a physiological readout rather than a surrogate for metabolic relief. We define a relief window as transient attenuation of hypoxic constraint accompanied by redistribution of lactate and adenosine away from T-cell-containing regions. Because such windows are short relative to ICB-driven reinvigoration, their therapeutic relevance may depend on recurrent temporal overlap, quantified through coverage and placement using provisional criteria at graded levels of evidence. The framework is proposed to apply primarily to glycolytic, hypoxic tumors retaining reinvigoration-competent progenitor exhausted T cells, with KRAS/STK11 co-mutant and KEAP1-altered NSCLC prioritized for testing as indicators of metabolic phenotype rather than predictors of benefit, subject to baseline confirmation that a reinvigoration-competent T-cell compartment is present. We specify necessary conditions, enabling requirements, and failure conditions, together with safety monitoring for repeated heating, while treating local-to-systemic immune propagation as an optional extension. A phase 0 strategy is proposed to establish whether reproducible candidate relief windows can be detected in patients, before efficacy testing and before any inference of clinical benefit.

title: Integrated Computational Pipeline Combining Metabolomics and Network Pharmacology for Bioactive Scaffold Discovery: Application to Antarctic Moss Chorisodontium aciphyllum.
authors: Yamaguchi H, Park HS, Yamada R et al.
abstract: Discovering lead compounds from complex natural matrices traditionally requires resource-intensive isolation steps. Integrating computational biology with untargeted metabolomics offers a more efficient alternative for rapid target prediction and screening. Here, we present a computational pipeline combining LC-MS/MS metabolomics, network pharmacology, and molecular docking to identify bioactive scaffolds. We applied this approach to the methanolic extract of the Antarctic moss Chorisodontium aciphyllum as a model matrix. Profiling the bioactive fraction (Fr.3) identified 17 secondary metabolites, primarily featuring fatty acid and steroidal scaffolds. Network pharmacology and functional annotation predicted ERBB2 and AKT1 as key protein targets for anti-lung cancer activity. Molecular docking supported these predictions, showing that steroidal and secosteroidal compounds such as 5α-ergosta-7,22-diene-3β,5-diol and 25-hydroxyvitamin D2 exhibit high binding affinities to these targets. As a preliminary in vitro validation of the computationally predicted pathways, we found that Fr.3 significantly increased intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels and induced apoptosis-mediated cell death in LLC1 murine lung cancer cells (IC50 ≈ 45.79 µg/mL). Our findings demonstrate that combining untargeted metabolomics with computational analysis can effectively streamline the discovery of therapeutic leads from uncharacterized natural extracts.

title: Primary Cervical Diffuse Large B-cell Lymphoma Incidentally Diagnosed During Evaluation of High-Grade Cervical Dysplasia: A Case Report.
authors: Anyadibe A, Javed Z, Stephenson M et al.
abstract: Primary diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the uterine cervix is a rare extranodal malignancy that may mimic more common cervical pathologies. We report the case of a 33-year-old woman with human papillomavirus (HPV)-16 positivity who was found to have cervical DLBCL incidentally during evaluation and treatment of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (HSIL). Histopathologic analysis following repeat excisional procedure revealed DLBCL, germinal center B-cell subtype, without residual epithelial dysplasia. Staging positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) demonstrated fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake confined to the cervix and central uterine cavity, without nodal or distant involvement. Bone marrow and endometrial biopsies were negative. The disease was classified as stage IE extranodal DLBCL with low-risk features. The patient was treated with four cycles of R-CHOP (rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone) using a PET-adapted approach based on the Intergroup S1001 trial and achieved a complete metabolic response. This case highlights an uncommon presentation of cervical lymphoma, the importance of accurate histopathologic diagnosis, and the role of PET-adapted therapy in limited-stage disease.

title: Modulation of G6PD-mediated Vitamin C Sensitivity in Small Cell Lung Cancer by the AKT/NRF2 axis.
authors: Yao X, Lyu Y, Zhang Z et al.
abstract: Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) remains a highly lethal malignancy with limited therapeutic advances. Although high-dose vitamin C (Vc) exhibits anti-tumor activity in various cancers, its therapeutic potential and underlying resistance mechanisms in SCLC remain poorly understood. Here, we identified heterogeneous responses to Vc among SCLC cell lines and found that Vc-resistant cells acquire enhanced antioxidant capacity to tolerate Vc-induced oxidative stress. Through transcriptomic, multi-omics, and functional analyses, we identified glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) as a critical determinant of Vc resistance. Mechanistically, Vc activates the p-AKT/p-GSK3β/NRF2 signaling axis in resistant cells, leading to NRF2-dependent transcriptional upregulation of G6PD and activation of antioxidant adaptation programs. Integrated analyses of transcriptomic, proteomic, single-cell, and spatial transcriptomic datasets further supported the involvement of the NRF2-G6PD axis in oxidative stress adaptation in SCLC. Importantly, pharmacological inhibition of G6PD with RRx-001 restored Vc sensitivity and synergistically suppressed SCLC growth in vitro and in vivo. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism underlying Vc resistance in SCLC and demonstrate that co-targeting G6PD provides a potential strategy to enhance the therapeutic efficacy of Vc.

title: [Atypical Pulmonary Carcinoid with Multiple Distant Metastases Treated with Primary Tumor Resection].
authors: Abe K, Matsuura Y, Sato K et al.
abstract: A 73-year-old man presented with cough and was found to have a tumor in the right lower lobe associated with obstructive pneumonia. Chest computed tomography (CT) and fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography revealed multiple distant metastases involving the liver, lymph nodes, and bone. Bronchoscopic biopsy suggested typical pulmonary carcinoid. Although curative resection was not feasible, primary tumor resection was performed to achieve local control and prevent recurrent obstructive pneumonia. Histopathological examination demonstrated atypical pulmonary carcinoid. The patient subsequently received carboplatin plus etoposide, followed by everolimus and a somatostatin analogue after disease progression. Local control was achieved, and the patient's general condition has been maintained despite slow progression of liver metastases. This case suggests that primary tumor resection may be a useful treatment option in selected patients with metastatic atypical pulmonary carcinoid.

title: Tumor Longevity: a time-dependent biomarker of immune checkpoint inhibitor responsiveness across head and neck, lung, renal and urothelial cancers.
authors: Romanò R, Airoldi C, Alfieri S et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND: the duration of tumor persistence within the host-defined as Tumor Longevity (TL) - may capture cumulative biological and immunologic interactions, shaping immunotherapy treatment response. However, the impact of TL on outcomes with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) remains unexplored. We hypothesized that TL may reflect integrated tumor-host dynamics influencing ICI efficacy and investigated this association in patients with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), renal and urothelial cancer (R/UC).
MATERIALS AND METHODS: we conducted a retrospective, observational study including adult patients with advanced HNSCC, NSCLC, R/UC receiving ICI (≥first line) across 2 Italian cancer centers. TL, defined as the time from first histological diagnosis to ICI initiation, was analyzed as a continuous variable using 3-knot restricted cubic spline models. Multivariable logistic and Cox regression analyses assessed associations between TL and disease control rate (DCR), grade (G)≥3 immune-related adverse events (irAEs), and overall survival (OS).
RESULTS: 304 patients, diagnosed from 2002 to 2022, started ICI from 2014 to 2022. Median TL was 15.30 months (IQR 5.52-33.05). Overall DCR was 56.25% [95% CI 50.47; 61.91]; CTCAE G ≥ 3 irAEs occurred in 16 (5.2%) patients; 231 (76.0%) patients died. In multivariable analyses, longer TL was associated with higher DCR (OR Q3 vs. Q1 = 3.26; 95%CI 1.24; 8.59, p = 0.004), while no significant associations for G ≥ 3 irAEs (OR = 1.27; 95% CI 0.39-4.12) and OS (HR = 0.79; 95% CI 0.49-1.28; p = 0.407) were observed.
CONCLUSIONS: These real-world, hypothesis-raising results suggest that TL may capture clinically relevant information associated with ICI outcomes. TL may represent a pragmatic, time-dependent biomarker integrating tumor behavior and host factors. Prospective and translational studies incorporating TL with molecular and immune profiling are warranted to elucidate whether this association reflects tumor biology, host factors, treatment history, or their combination.

title: CT imaging biomarkers after neoadjuvant immunotherapy in resectable non-small cell lung cancer: from response assessment to surgical decision-making.
authors: Li Y, Wen L
abstract: Neoadjuvant immune checkpoint blockade, usually combined with platinum-based chemotherapy, has improved pathologic response and event-free survival in patients with resectable non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC). Preoperative assessment remains difficult, however, because radiographic change does not directly represent the amount of residual viable tumor. Immune-cell infiltration, edema, necrosis, granulomatous nodal reactions, and reparative fibrosis may preserve tumor size despite major or complete pathologic response, whereas small viable tumor nests may remain within an apparently fibrotic bed. This Mini Review examines computed tomography (CT) biomarkers after neoadjuvant immunotherapy, focusing on conventional and dual-energy CT, radiomics, delta-radiomics, and deep-learning models. Size-based response criteria are reproducible but insufficient for tissue characterization. Selected, predominantly retrospective studies suggest that temporal models can add information, but transportability and clinical utility remain uncertain. We distinguish four intended uses: pathologic-response prediction, nodal restaging, technical resectability and operative-complexity assessment, and prognosis. Conventional CT informs anatomy and complication assessment; quantitative response models remain investigational. Suspicious new or enlarging nodes warrant tissue confirmation when the result would alter curative surgery. A structured reporting checklist links imaging uncertainty to multidisciplinary action. Imaging biomarkers should complement clinical, pathologic, and molecular data and should not currently be used to omit surgery.

title: Case Report: Pembrolizumab-associated airway-predominant relapsing polychondritis with longitudinal CD8+ T-cell activation and bronchial stenting.
authors: Xia C, Chen J, Fang X et al.
abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) can trigger autoimmune and autoinflammatory toxicities through disruption of peripheral immune tolerance. Relapsing polychondritis (RP) after programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1) blockade is rare and are described mainly in individual reports. We report a 66-year-old man who developed severe airway-predominant RP after 10 cycles of pembrolizumab for lung adenocarcinoma. Chest CT showed new diffuse tracheal and bilateral bronchial wall thickening and calcification, with severe obstructive ventilatory impairment and systemic inflammation. Exploratory serial peripheral-blood immunophenotyping demonstrated increased proportions of CD38+ and HLA-DR+ cells among circulating CD8+ T cells early in the disease course. Serial measurements showed lower activated CD8+ T-cell proportions during immunosuppressive treatment, in parallel with partial stabilization of respiratory symptoms, pulmonary function and imaging. The patient received sequential glucocorticoids, tofacitinib, methotrexate, abatacept and tocilizumab. Despite partial inflammatory control, subsequent pulmonary infection with severe coughing was followed by pneumomediastinum and progressive structural airway compromise requiring bilateral main-bronchial stenting. One year after stenting, the stents remained in situ with no obvious luminal stenosis and pulmonary function remained stable. This case extends the reported spectrum of pembrolizumab-associated RP by documenting an airway-predominant, treatment refractory course with serial immune phenotyping and long-term post-stenting follow-up.

title: Patient-Specific MRD Liquid Biopsy in Resected NSCLC: Plasma and Bronchial Washing ctDNA
interventions: Patient-specific tumor-informed MRD assay (plasma and bronchial washing ctDNA)
Bronchoscopy with bronchial washing for reserach
summary: This is a multicenter, prospective, observational pilot cohort study in patients with surgically resected non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC, pathologic stage IA3-IIIA). Whole exome sequencing (WES) of each patient's resected tumor tissue and matched normal blood (buffy coat) is used to build a patient-specific (tumor-informed) minimal residual disease (MRD) panel, after excluding germline and clonal hematopoiesis variants. MRD is then assessed in paired plasma circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and bronchial washing fluid (BWF) ctDNA collected at 6, 12, 18 and 24 months after surgery. The study evaluates whether MRD positivity in plasma and/or BWF is associated with subsequent clinical or radiologic recurrence, compares MRD detection rates and quantitative values between plasma and BWF, and explores the lead time of MRD detection relative to standard surveillance with chest CT and serum CEA. MRD results are not used to confirm recurrence or to change treatment; all clinical decisions follow standard of care. Forty participants will be enrolled at three Severance hospitals in Korea.

summary: This is an open-label, multi-centre, phase 3 randomised controlled trial comparing 4 weeks with 6 weeks of Chemoradiotherapy (CRT) followed by consolidation immunotherapy in patients with unresectable, non-targetable stage 3 NSCLC given with curative intent.

title: Image-guided lung ablation: Experience at an intermediate complexity centre.
authors: Castell Herrera A, Morales García M, Alonso Diego I et al.
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVE: Lung cancer in patients with inoperability criteria has been increasing in recent years. For these patients, other less invasive therapeutic options such as thermal ablation or stereotactic radiotherapy are being considered. The aim of the study is to analyse the outcomes of thermal ablation for malignant lung lesions in terms of survival and complications at an intermediate complexity centre over a 10-year period.
MATERIAL AND METHODS: A retrospective observational review was conducted of computed tomography-guided lung ablations performed between 2012 and 2022 using radiofrequency, microwave or cryoablation. Survival rates were calculated, and lesion characteristics were described along with the main identified complications.
RESULTS: A total of 25 tumour lesions were ablated, with a mean size of 15.8 mm (range: 8-28 mm), including both primary and metastatic lesions. The most common immediate complication was pneumothorax (36%). The most severe complication was bronchopleural fistula, with a post-procedural mortality rate of 4%. Local progression-free survival rates were 91%, 71% and 64% at 6, 12 and 24 months, respectively. The mean overall survival time was 40 months.
CONCLUSIONS: Thermal ablative therapies are well-tolerated procedures, with good survival rates and a low likelihood of complications.

title: Combining handcrafted radiomics features and deep learning features within different regions of interest in planning CT images for the prediction of symptomatic radiation pneumonitis in locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer.
authors: Li X, Hang H, Kong Y et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: To predict symptomatic radiation pneumonitis (RP) in locally advanced non-small cell lung cancer (LA-NSCLC) patients by handcrafted radiomics (HCR) and deep learning (DL) features of three different regions of interest (ROIs) in normal lung tissue.
METHODS: Ninety LA-NSCLC patients from Center A were collected as the development cohort, and an additional 57 patients from Center B were collected as the external validation set. Clinical data and lung dose-volume parameters were collected from the patients, and univariate analysis was conducted. Three ROIs in lung were delineated in pre-radiotherapy CT images: Lung-PTV, Lung-GTV, and PTV-GTV. For each ROI, 1046 HCR features and 512 DL features were respectively extracted, and then correlated. For each ROI, three models (HCR, DLR, and a hybrid model) were developed with feature selection via Spearman correlation, mRMR, the LASSO method, and SVM-based modeling. And finally, their performance was evaluated and compared using AUC values from ROC curves. The optimal model was selected by comparing the best AUC through internal validation results, and then external validation was conducted. Calibration and decision curve analyses were used to evaluate the model.
RESULTS: In the development cohort, univariate analysis revealed no statistically significant associations with RP. The correlation analysis revealed a weak correlation between HCR and DL features. In internal validation, for Lung-PTV, Lung-GTV and PTV-GTV, HCR models achieved AUCs of 0.658 (95%CI: 0.645-0.671), 0.659 (95%CI: 0.646-0.672), and 0.890 (95%CI: 0.881-0.899); DLR models obtained AUCs of 0.832 (95%CI: 0.824-0.840), 0.900 (95%CI: 0.893-0.907), and 0.777 (95%CI: 0.766-0.788); and the hybrid model showed AUCs of 0.838 (95%CI: 0.831-0.846), 0.901 (95%CI: 0.894-0.908), and 0.919 (95%CI: 0.912-0.926). The results showed that the DLR model outperformed the HCR model for Lung-PTV and Lung-GTV, and the hybrid model surpassed both for all three ROIs. The hybrid model of PTV-GTV was found to be the best, and its external validation was conducted. The results showed that the AUC for the external validation set was 0.828 (95%CI: 0.696-0.960). The model was well calibrated (p > 0.05), and decision curve analysis indicated positive net benefit across relevant threshold probabilities.
CONCLUSIONS: Hybrid models combining HCR and DL features showed the highest predictive performance in internal comparisons and the best-performing PTV-GTV hybrid model was externally validated, highlighting the potential of combined features for improved prediction.

title: Multiomics Analysis of Malignant Pleural Mesothelioma Reveals the Immunological Microenvironment Associated with MTAP Loss and Immunotherapy Outcomes.
authors: Tateishi A, Yoshida T, Shiraishi K et al.
abstract:
PURPOSE: Nivolumab plus ipilimumab is a standard first-line therapy for unresectable malignant pleural mesothelioma (MPM), yet biomarkers predicting immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) efficacy remain undefined. We aimed to identify genomic and tumor immune microenvironmental features associated with ICI response in MPM.
EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN: We analyzed two independent MPM cohorts. The discovery cohort included patients at the National Cancer Center Hospital (2012-2022) with frozen tumor tissues available for whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and RNA sequencing. Genomic alterations, transcriptomic profiles, immune cell composition, and T-cell receptor repertoire were analyzed, and key findings were validated in a nationwide Center for Cancer Genomics and Advanced Therapeutics (C-CAT) cohort.
RESULTS: The WGS cohort comprised 52 patients. Among ICI-treated patients, overall response rates were 30% in the WGS cohort and 29.4% in the C-CAT cohort. Genomic analyses identified frequent alterations in BAP1 and NF2, across both cohorts. ICI responders showed higher T-cell receptor diversity, increased CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration, and enrichment of M1 macrophages compared with non-responders. MTAP loss was associated with higher CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration and T-cell receptor diversity, and was linked to a higher ICI response rate in the C-CAT cohort. In contrast, BAP1 and NF2 alterations showed no consistent association with immune features or ICI efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: An immune-active tumor microenvironment characterized by high T-cell receptor diversity, CD8⁺ T-cell infiltration, and M1 macrophage enrichment was associated with favorable ICI responses in MPM. MTAP loss was linked to immune-related features and a higher ICI response, supporting further investigation of MTAP loss as a candidate biomarker.

title: Integrated Multi-Omics Profiling of Thymoma Identifies Subtype-Specific Remodeling and Myasthenia Gravis-Associated Targets.
authors: Sun Y, Mao J, Sun X et al.
abstract: Thymoma is a rare thymic epithelial tumor strongly associated with myasthenia gravis (MG), yet the tumor intrinsic molecular states underlying this link remain unclear. Here, we profiled paired thymoma and distant nontumorous thymic tissues using untargeted metabolomics, lipidomics, and label-free quantitative proteomics, integrating these layers with MG status, clinicopathologic data, immunohistochemistry, and external transcriptomic validation from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) cohort. Thymomas exhibited a reproducible metabolic and lipidomic signature characterized by coordinated alterations in amino acid and nucleotide metabolism alongside structured changes in lipid subclasses that support membrane remodeling. Proteomic profiling distinguished tumors from distant nontumorous thymic tissue and identified three exploratory proteomic groups with distinct pathway patterns tightly coupled to lipid metabolic shifts. Integrated analyses identified HMGCS1 and SCP2 as subtype-enriched, lipid-linked hubs and uncovered an MG-associated molecular module comprising creatine, MePC(37:4), ACP5, AP1S1, NECTIN4, and fatty acid pathways. AP1S1 showed an independent association with the overall survival in the TCGA thymoma cohort. A derived 13-lipid panel showed high discrimination in an internal evaluation, supporting its potential as a candidate signature for further validation. This tissue-based multi-omics study systematically maps coordinated molecular remodeling in thymoma, highlighting HMGCS1, SCP2, and AP1S1 as prioritized candidates for future mechanistic and translational research.

title: Agentic Discovery Transfer Enables Cross-Cancer Discovery at Scale.
authors: Cheng L, Shireman J, Gogate A et al.
abstract: Cancer research generates tens of thousands of studies each year, yet whether a published finding holds in another cancer type or patient population is rarely tested as doing so is labor-intensive and difficult to scale. We define this task as discovery transfer and present SMART, a multi-agent large language model framework for discovery transfer in single-cell RNA-sequencing studies. Given a source manuscript and a target dataset, SMART extracts major clinical and mechanistic findings, generates and executes analyses for the testable findings, reports which findings transfer, and suggests follow-up. Applied to 121 studies across six cancer types, SMART identified findings that transfer across cancers, including a lung cancer prognostic signature that we confirmed to be associated with survival in liver cancer, pancreatic cancer and pleural mesothelioma. SMART also generated new mechanistic hypotheses, demonstrating how agentic discovery transfer can extend published findings beyond their original setting.

title: Clinical-MRI-IVIM combined model for differentiating thymic epithelial tumors from anterior mediastinal lymphoma in large masses.
authors: Chen J, Tang W, Qi L et al.
abstract:
OBJECTIVES: To evaluate the diagnostic value of clinical and intravoxel incoherent motion (IVIM) parameters for differentiating large anterior mediastinal invasive masses (≥ 3 cm), particularly thymic epithelial tumors (TETs) and lymphomas.
METHODS: This prospective study included 92 patients (mean age, 44.8 ± 15.5 years) with pathologically confirmed TETs (n = 52) or lymphomas (n = 40) who underwent routine MRI, diffusion-weighted imaging, and IVIM sequences. Quantitative parameters, including the apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC), true diffusion coefficient (D), pseudo-diffusion coefficient (D*), and perfusion fraction (f), were measured. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were used to construct predictive models. Diagnostic performance was evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, with area under the curve (AUC) compared by the DeLong test. Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling, and multicollinearity was assessed using variance inflation factors.
RESULTS: Compared with TET, lymphoma was associated with younger age, higher female proportion, higher LDH, larger volume, more frequent pleural and/or lung invasion, and higher D * values (all p < 0.05). Age, sex, LDH level, lung and/or pleural infiltration, and f in the IVIM model were risk predictive factors for distinguishing lymphoma from TET. Among all models, the clinical MRI-IVM model achieved the highest diagnostic performance numerically (AUC = 0.946, 95% CI: 0.901-0.991); However, compared with the clinical MRI model (AUC = 0.929, 95% CI: 0.873-0.985), the increment brought by adding IVIM parameters was not significant (DeLong test, P = 0.316). Calibration analysis showed good consistency between predicted probabilities. The apparent AUC of Bootstrap's internal validation was 0.946, the estimation deviation was 0.017, and the standard error was 0.022, indicating limited optimism in the model's performance.
CONCLUSIONS: The clinical-MRI-IVIM model had shown relatively good diagnostic performance in preoperative differentiation of large anterior mediastinal TETs and lymphoma. However, there is no statistical difference in the increment benefit generated by IVIM parameters in the composite model. Therefore, in order to elucidate the clinical efficacy of IVIM, further large-scale, prospective, and multi-center studies are necessary.

title: [Recurrent Thymoma Responding to Low-dose Corticosteroid Therapy:Report of a Case].
authors: Abe K, Sato K, Minowa M
abstract: We report a rare case of recurrent thymoma that responded to low-dose corticosteroid therapy. A 54-year-old woman underwent extended thymectomy for invasive thymoma (World Health Organization classification type AB, Masaoka stage III). Despite multiple treatments, including radiotherapy, surgical resection of pleural dissemination, and chemotherapy with S-1 and carboplatin plus paclitaxel, the tumor showed progressive disease. At 71 years of age, low-dose prednisolone (5-20 mg/day) was incidentally administered for a dermatologic condition. Subsequently, marked tumor regression was observed on chest radiography without any additional anticancer treatment. Tumor control was maintained with 10 mg/day prednisolone. The patient later died of sepsis unrelated to thymoma progression. This case suggests that even low-dose corticosteroids may exert clinically significant antitumor effects in thymoma, particularly in refractory cases.

title: [Current State of the Asbestos Outpatient Clinic and an Evaluation of Asbestos Bodies].
authors: Ohta Y, Fujimori H, Kurose N et al.
abstract: A total of 46 cases visited our hospital's asbestos outpatient clinic over 12-year period from May 2013 to April 2025. The reasons for referral were as follows:15 cases were referred by the Labor Bureau, 15 by other departments within our hospital, 10 by other medical institutions, and six were self-referred. A history of asbestos exposure was identified in 40 cases (87%). Nine patients underwent surgery for asbestos-related malignancies (five primary lung cancers and four pleural mesotheliomas). In two lung cancer patients who underwent lobectomy, high concentrations of asbestos bodies were detected in non-cancerous lung tissue using a tissue digestion method, whereas none were identified by Berlin blue staining of routine sections. The diagnosis of asbestos-related lung cancer in general hospitals remains challenging.

title: [Surgical Case of Primary Malignant Pericardial Mesothelioma].
authors: Mieno S, Kishida K, Suzumura Y et al.
abstract: A 58-year-old male presented with floating sensation and hypotention during hemodialysis. Imaging studies demonstrated a tumor compressing the right ventricle resulting in cardiac tamponade. He underwent surgical tumor resection and partial pericardiectomy. The tumor was not completely resected because of tight adhesion between tumor and cardiac tissue around the right atrial appendage. The tumor was diagnosed with primary malignant pericardial mesothelioma (PMPM) by pathological studies. After surgery, he was free from cardiac tamponade. Three months after surgery, fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) did not detect abnormal accumulation to be suspected as the residual tumor and/or recurrence of PMPM. He remained alive and asymptomatic for 3.7 year after surgery. The effectiveness of surgery for PMPM is not clearly demonstrated because of its rarity, usually late presentation, and progressive nature of PMPM. In this case report we discussed about the characteristics and surgical results for PMPM in Japan.

title: A novel KIR3DL2-directed CAR T-cell therapy for cutaneous and systemic T-cell lymphomas
summary: Chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of B-cell malignancies and multiple myeloma, but its extension to T-cell lymphomas (TCLs) has been constrained by the paucity of antigens that can be safely targeted. While targeting pan-T antigens broadens the therapeutic reach across various TCLs, it carries a substantial risk of immunosuppression and infection. Here, we report killer cell immunoglobulin-like receptor, three Ig domains and long cytoplasmic tail 2 (KIR3DL2/CD158k) as a viable target for CAR T-cell therapy against a wide range of TCLs. Using single-cell RNA-seq data analysis and flow cytometric phenotyping, we observed that KIR3DL2 expression is restricted to a subset of mature NK cells and a minor fraction of CD8 T cells, with negligible expression in other healthy adult tissues. Among TCLs, KIR3DL2 expression was noted in various subtypes of cutaneous and systemic TCLs. Anti-KIR3DL2 CAR constructs (3DL2CARs) efficiently and selectively redirected T cells against antigen-positive cell lines but not isogenic KIR3DL2-negative counterparts, with antigen-specific signaling, cytotoxicity, proliferation, and cytokine production. Importantly, 3DL2CART cells produced sustained tumor regression and prolonged survival in two distinct cell line-derived xenograft models of cutaneous TCL and in one patient-derived xenograft model of hepatosplenic TCL. 3DL2CART cells exhibited minimal off-target activity against bystander immune cells and showed no appreciable fratricide. To mitigate the risk of tumor cell contamination in autologous CAR T-cell products, we established a two-tiered strategy that integrates immunomagnetic depletion of KIR3DL2-positive tumor cells with in vivo activation of a safety switch if inadvertently transduced malignant cells contribute to immune escape.
